This game shows its age, but that doesn't stop it from being fun! 
Lots you can do in character creation. You can save outfit presets, and edit your crew members to a surprising extent. All very roleplayer friendly! :D

If you are someone easily overwhelmed trying to learn to navigate a bunch of menus/interfaces I'm afraid this game will have a steep learning curve there. At least the layouts are logical, include tool tips, and (thank god) much of what you'll be doing is in one menu (default U).

The ground combat is simple at first, though if you want more aiming involved you can do that by pressing B.
The space combat is deceptively simple and slow (I kind of feel like that 1st multi-ship battle might be a little too tough for a tutorial but that's subjective ). 
Best part: the tutorial stage of the game is super forgiving! I still felt a bit rushed to do the mission but I eventually realized I was not in much danger if I took a moment to hover over buttons to try and understand it.

The bad?: [list]
[*]sometimes the tutorial and mission voices over will play at the same time. Some tutorials repeat themselves....A LOT. I've not figured out how to make it shut up yet.
[*] I haven't found if I can turn off double tap to dodge. Good for avoiding aoes but it's ridiculously sensitive. 
[*]Warping to other systems are kind of a hassle. Fortunately you can set the ship to fly itself there while you play around in menus.
[*] What ARE the rewards of creating a character in a faction during a temporal event? I shouldn't have to put as much research effort as I did to find the answer.
[/list]

Overall, the plot missions I have played are quite good any Star Trek fan will likely feel a hint of the Star Trek shows of the 1990s and beyond.

I personally have progressed to Commander with access to epic starfleet ships and have not paid a dime.  
There is a currency you pay for: Zen, that can be used to buy some ships (so far, not the key ones you see in the shows/movies) and clothing.  You can get Zen using the same currency to get extra ships, so technically you can play it for free forever.

In conclusion, this is a most worthy freemium game for any star trek fan.  I highly recommend it.

I played this game for several years on PS4 and absolutely loved it. However, on PC, the UI is absurd. It's hard to see anything that's going on, especially in space, because there is just so much crap on screen at all times. Everything just ran so much smoother on console, from movement to combat to inventory management. It just blows my mind that a game like this is 100% better on console than PC. The devs don't seem to listen to their community at all either. They just keep adding paid content, despite everyone asking for fixes and UI improvements. They say PC has FULL controller support, but it's more like 25% controller support, which is completely ridiculous considering there are no issues using a controller on console, and they won't even acknowledge you if you ask about that. It's a good thing this game is entirely free. It's a good game, and I enjoy playing it, when I am able, but it would not be worth paying for, and devs that don't care about their community don't deserve our money. If they would focus on improving gameplay, and stop worrying about adding new ships that nobody wanted or asked for, that you have to pay for, this game could easily be one of the best games available.

"Delta Rising" propels you into the far future, where the galaxy faces new threats and opportunities. "Agents of Yesterday" is a fantastic throwback for fans of classic Trek. It lets you step into the boots of a Starfleet officer from the 23rd century, providing a nostalgic journey filled with iconic references and classic Starship designs. It's a perfect blend of old-school charm and modern gameplay, and a must-play for any Trek aficionado.

The regular updates and seasonal events keep the game feeling fresh, offering everything from exciting new missions to special in-game events that celebrate the ever-expanding lore of Star Trek. The social aspect of the game is also worth noting; joining a fleet and collaborating with other players adds layers of strategy and camaraderie that enhance the overall experience.

Star Trek Online isn’t just a game; it’s a living, breathing homage to the Star Trek universe. With its ever-expanding content, deep lore, and engaging gameplay, it offers a rich, immersive experience that allows you to explore strange new worlds, seek out new life and civilizations, and boldly go where no gamer has gone before.

If you enjoy Star Trek, you'll like it. You get to be your own character--as is to be expected of an MMORPG--but the depth you're able to customize your characters in is almost ridiculous. The only complaint I have in that regard is that some of the more notable uniform designs are locked behind a paywall. You also get to customize your ship quite a lot too, with the TNG. DS9 and Voyager ship types of Galaxy class, Defiant class and Intrepid class being unlocked at the rank of Captain. The respective bridge designs are generally only for the specific type of ship--galaxy is an engineering ship, defiant a tactical and intrepid a science. However. you can pay for a one-to-one replication of the show bridges if you want--as an example--a tactical ship with an engineering bridge. 

Additionally, you also get some pretty nice cameos from Star Trek actors from just about every show except--to my knowledge--ST Enterprise.  The story arcs are really fun and engaging, with away missions and ship battles being insanely fun--unless your under level. 

So, if you enjoy Star Trek adventures, role playing, or just enjoy dressing up a character, this game is really fun, and you should try it out.

PS: It's also rather cool that the solar system is actually relatively accurate to how it actually is. Uranus has its really weird axis, and Neptune and again Uranus are both the correct color. These details actually made my Astrophysics professor really happy when I told him about them.

I played Star Trek Online at launch, and, well, it felt like someone put the holodeck on "Malfunction Mode." Ground combat? Let’s just say it was like trying to win a dance-off with a Klingon—awkward, slow, and painful. I quit faster than Kirk dodging a Klingon b'day party.

But recently, some friends dragged me back into it, and I’m kind of glad they did. Space combat? Its pretty fun. It’s like flying the Enterprise into battle—minus the weekly moral dilemma. The ships still look great. Sure, you can tell the game is as old as a Vulcan’s favorite meditation practice, but those ships still look sharp enough to cut through Spock’s logic.

And let’s talk about science vessels. These things have more space magic than Gandalf at a hobbit bachelor party. You’ll be throwing out enough glowing orbs and beams to look like you’re DJing a rave in the middle of a nebula. Honestly, it’s so over the top, you might want a pair of sunglasses just to play it safely.

The community is generally friendly and still fairly active. You hop into group content, and boom—you’re off on a mission faster than Scotty can say, “I’m giving her all she’s got!”

But then there’s the ground combat. Let’s be real—it’s still terrible. You feel like you’re stuck in slow motion, waving a phaser around like a child with a toy lightsaber, except the enemies might not even notice. If you ever wanted to know what it's like to fight with a Tricorder in one hand and regret in the other, here’s your chance!

All in all, Star Trek Online still has its quirks (seriously, did I mention ground combat?), but if you’re into space battles, techno-magic, and starships that look like they just rolled out of the shipyard, it’s worth revisiting. Give her all she's got, just don’t beam down too often.

[h2]The Game’s Got Legs; Shame about the (Inter)Face[/h2]

I’ve been spending a lot of my free time in this game now. Time that I normally would have been putting into EVE Online but given that they’re not doing anything to let gamers opt out of PvP I’ve given them up for dead. The very idea of putting yourself at risk every time you go to mine some ore or go play a mission is just a dumb model for gaming, pure and simple. Especially when mining ore is (in a word) boring. The fact that they’re just sitting on that problem led me on a search for some other game to play that was worthy of my time.

I’ll be up front – EVE had pretty much put me off MMOs. I figured that the only people who got value out of them were the little nobodies who spent their entire lives on the game ganking other players just for the fun of it. Ruining other people’s experiences just to enhance their own self-esteem.

That said, I’d had STO in my library and never tried it before. I tried it. So much closer to what I wanted from an MMO experience. Certainly not the sociopath incubating zero trust environment of EVE. More of an immersive experience rooted in the ST universe.

Starting out was tough, but then every MMO is tough until you get your head around all the complexity that they’ve added and how it all works and fits together. Inside a month I was at the top of the level tree (Fleet Admiral 65) and having a ball. I’ve now pretty much played out all the episodes (yeah, episodes. Each looks like a mission but tells a story) for all the arcs that are out there and I sit and do task force operations (PvE Co-Op team missions) to stay in the game and wait for more content to come out in the form of events. That’s the real point of it being an MMO – they keep creating new content for it.

That content includes voice acting by actual ST character actors who appear in the story arcs as they’re developed. You get to see new takes on what various characters are doing or have done, and you get to see them all integrated in some fashion with a current timeline, usually through temporal operations and the like, but they’re there and that is the most important thing. The developers are making this world as immersive as they can by adding characters you can relate to and interact with, at least in the context of mission delivery.

It’s mostly single or co-op team play but they do release some PvP content for those who want to do that. The important thing is that the PvP is opt in, not (can’t) opt-out or any other model. Like all good co-op systems, you have the chance to respawn (so you’re not putting your stuff at risk) which makes sense in a ST environment – all your stuff can essentially be replicated again, right? But, it also makes sense because you only earn ships through certain events and the rank system. Every other ship you’re going to own, you’re going to buy. Either through resources in-game, or with Zen, which is effectively in-game cash that you’ve paid for with real world currency. Who wants to pay $30 US for a ship only to have some griefer blow it up 30 seconds after you leave spacedock? No-one would support that so in effect, the ships you either earn or buy are better thought of as ship templates.

The social aspect of it is minimal, or at least it was for me because I was actively looking to avoid it. If knowing about the social model is important to you, go read reviews written by Gen Ys or Millenials. They know about that kind of thing.

I did however join a fleet because my toon kept getting fleet join requests that I had to go out of my way to decline. In the end one came through with an interesting name that I could relate to so I accepted. That’s the last I’ve heard of any of them, or of anyone else wanting me to join them. That said, it turns out the fleet gives you some minor boosts in the game and you can contribute to fleet assets like colonies and starbases that you can visit (and use to certain levels) in the game.

Generally speaking, I have to say that it is an enjoyable experience that can be a little overly complex in my opinion, but I can live with that. Every large scale game that has been around long enough has complexity built in simply because of the organic nature of keeping itself relevant in a sea of changing wants and needs from an evolving player base.

What I find much harder to live with is the interface. It’s bad.

[b]BAD.[/b]

It doesn’t suck; sitting next to a bickering couple in a movie theatre sucks. This interface licks the slime off the scrotum of a three-weeks-dead llama carcass. If I was still teaching interface design and one of my second years put this in front of me, I’d not only fail them but I’d be looking for ways to get them kicked out of the uni for fear a future employer might ask ‘where is it you said you studied?’

Buttons keep jumping from the lower right corner of the screen to the lower centre, and then flipping back. They mask what’s going on in the fight when they’re centre. In TFOs, you can sometimes have to click a button on the lower right, then the centre, then in the lower left just to claim a single item. During combat, no less. The stacking of objects on the lower left push the current buttons up, so you can think you’re passing on something you don’t want only to find you’ve just passed up that one item you’ve been looking for because it took the place of the other one in the stack. There’s no ‘take all’ or ‘claim all’ buttons on any of the interfaces for combat, research, missions, et al. The inventory [i]sometimes[/i] stacks items of the same type, with no logic I can see as to why. Claiming on duty officer missions requires you to keep changing your mouse location because the claim button will be at a different height depending on the length of the mission name. At least they stack; research and admiralty systems force you to go to each slot, which again moves as the empty slots are thinner than the full ones (and by different sizes). Searching is either non-existent or a joke.

Cryptic - get your interface design team to actually play the game. Put it in their employment contracts that they have to play the game for at least 8hrs per week, and I’m not talking about opening the inventory once every 15 mins so the idle checkers don’t trip. Play the game and interact with all parts of it that require you to interact with a different interface. If they can’t see what’s wrong after a month of that; sack them. They’re not doing you any favours.

Another point that I want to make here is that there is a gambling element to this game and you need to consider that before you buy into it. They give away lock boxes, but you have to buy the keys. For actual money (via Zen). Each key opens a box with a chance of an epic prize of a great ship, but a lot more [i]not[/i]-epic prizes. Arguably, there should be gambler warnings on the purchase of things like master keys. They’ve certainly got public announcements when someone wins an epic prize. If you have a gambling addiction, this is not your game.

One other area that needs a [b]LOT[/b] more attention is starship internals. Currently they’re great but you can’t really do anything there. I’ve got a massive captain’s cabin that allows me to do precisely nothing inside it. I can’t even sit in the chairs. I can’t put my toon to sleep in the bed. I can’t interact with it. Hell, the cabin itself (to scale) is bigger than my house. I’d love to be able to do things in it.

If gambling doesn’t phase you, if you can live with one of the worst interface disasters I’ve ever seen, and if you love star trek and can except that you’ll never see a light sabre in the game because of cross-over concerns (but let’s face it – a phaser sabre; [b]phabre[/b] if you will – would be an AWESOME addition, and given most scientists think that a plasma energy sword is more realistic than a laser sword, the Romulans should have this SO covered; again I digress), then you need to give this a try.

I've played this game for years and its fun. Its not the best game out there I don't even know if its qualifies as the best Star trek game but it does offer a good variety of freedom to create a character in the setting. Its the sheer amount of ships, costumes, weapons, missions and other gear is great. You can basically make any humanoid alien you want or play as a standard Star trek race like a vulcan or Klingon. This applies to your crew as well with you being able to customize your bridge crew including thier appearance, species, and uniform. 

Ships are where this game really shines though. A simply massive number of them many with custom traits and consoles that can be transfered to other ships. This can be anything from your standard federation saucer and klingon bird of prey to enigmatic alien vessels like the jellyfish from Farpoint. The only thing I do not like about the ship system is lockbox ships. These ships require you to open lockboxes which are just lootboxes and are CHARACTER bound. This means even if you get a lockbox ship on one character you do not have access to it on any others unless you buy it again. This does not apply to most other ships such as Zen store ships which require you to spend the premium currency and unlock account wide. Event ships are also account wide and feature some very unique and fun designs. Luckily in recent years they introduced Event campagins so even as a F2P player you can get the lockbox ships on at least one character without farming as absurd amount of Dilithium or EC. 

That brings me to the next virtue this game has. The exchange. Almost anything can be traded on the exchange. This includes lockbox ships provided they haven't been opened and claimed. This provides one of the only ways to get lockbox ships for F2P players. In addition event currency for the winter and summer events can be bought or sold on the exchange as well as certain unique weapons, consoles, even bridge crew. 

Space combat is 100% the more fun and focused of the two gameplay modes, the other being ground combat. The space combat just feels more polished and fluid than ground combat which tends to be rather stiff but it does have some fun moments. Its very satisfying to open up a broadside of phasers on an enemy ship or launch a full spread of torpedoes at a cluster of enemy ships. I esspecially love some console abilities which let you make crazy hazards in space like gravity wells, tears in reality, encase your enemies in energy webs or even shoot giant lasers from the front like some sort of super weapon.

This is an amazing game. Personally, the "Science" in star trek always bugged me. But this... this game, has amazingly satisfying space combat enhanced by the PhysX on my Nividia geforce RTX 3050 6GB Laptop edition. best of all, it has a lot for free players like me. i have no extra money to pay for anything, so there is all sorts of ways to get things for free. One character can refine about 8,000 Dilithium a day, (This is a semi-premium currency, used for all sorts of purchases, like spaceships, etc) and there is a way around this. if you have more than one character, you can go on your other characters and post all your refined diltihium on the dilithium exchange for a price no one will buy. Then, go onto the character you want all the dilithium on and cancel your posts on the exchange from all your other characters. Then withdraw all of it from the pool. This will make all the dilithium you refined that day go to one character. There is also Lobi Crystals. Again, Semi-premium currency, but you can get them from Events if you're a free player. These can be exchanged for Spaceships, consumables, you name it. Then there is Zen. This is a premium currency, one character can trade in 8,000 dilithium for roughly 10 Zen. + A lot of effort was put into in-game cutscenes, and that's kinda nice.

[h2]What's not so fun:[/h2]
- Ground and space combat could be refined, but is something you get used to. Though, it appears that it's not the focus
- Downloading the game is manageable, but returning to find the 'idle connection error', and the game didn't finish downloading its resources, sucks. At least, what was downloaded won't need to be downloaded again, but the download percentage won't show you that.
- Railroaded narrative, not branching off with different outcomes.
- Inventory doesn't feel cohesive. If I hover over an item I'd like to see a visual cue of the stat comparison between what I've equipped and the similar item type I'm looking at.  

[h2]Summary[/h2]
Despite the combat, if you love Star Trek and want to have a little taste of something that reminds you of those "strange, new worlds", and its themes of philosophy and morality with sci-fi spunk, you might enjoy this game as I do.
It's 7/10 for me.

As a Star Trek fan, STO truly feels like the last bastion of the kind of atmosphere and political intrigue classic Star Trek was all about, I know for many this will be reason enough to hop in but as a video game? My recommendation of STO has to be a bit more nuanced. 

Pros:

+ Extends the Prime Timeline Star Trek Universe with great stories
+ Many of the cast reprise their roles
+ Starship customisation and combat is fantastic 
+ Fully customisable bridge crew
+ Mountains of content
+ Hundreds of ships to choose from with a new one for free every 10 levels
+ Satisfying progression 
+ Mountains of PvE content 
+ All expansions are free and several release each year

Neutral:

~ PvE focused experience
~ Lots of paid content if you choose
~ Endgame is based on accruing reputation and other currencies
~ A medium-sized but very stable player base

Cons:

- Premium ships are very expensive
- Lifetime subscription is an extortionate lump sum payment
- Older content is dated and buggy
- Ship texture quality is uneven
- The factions outside of Starfleet and the Klingon Empire are half-baked or even abandoned 
- A history of removed features and vaulted content, some of which being fan-favourites
- Ground combat is boring and repetitive 

Summary: If you're a Trekkie then you should absolutely play this game for its brand of storytelling and the reprised voice roles; the whole thing plays like a particularly bloodthirsty episode of Deep Space 9 and the direction the story-lines take many characters in are unexpected but often very creative directions. This game is old, the playerbase size cannot compare to something like ESO, it lacks polish and the ground combat isn't very fun but I've never been invested in any other MMO like this one and where modern Trek TV just makes me sad for what once was, facing a Borg Cube in STO makes me smile for what's still alive.

THE GOOD:
Lots of content: Story, interaction, characters, action.

There are 2 kinds of battles: Ground or Space
Space Missions: You control a ship, which you will have many through the game. Currently Tier 6 (T6) ships are the best ships and there are hundreds of them to choose from.

The Bad: Story design can be frustrating. As you progress in the story missions, sometimes someone starts to talk to you, which covers almost the entire screen. And sometimes enemies start attacking you at the same time. So I either skip the dialogue missing the story content or just wait till they finish talking and miss the entire fight (My officers are great, they usually handle the fight on their own). 

Same, when you kill everyone on a level, a pop-up conversation forces you to leave the place, while the room is full of uncollected loot. VERY Frustrating. So now my priority is always to collect the loot while the enemy is shooting at me. 

This is an old game and it shows. Play it if you like complicated games, or just to shoot stuff (STO users call it pew pew... ) but only if you think you can handle some of the frustration of the bad game design and bugs.

If you like Star Trek, and I mean LIKE Star Trek, to the point where you've sought out and watched entire series, then this is the game for you. If you're seeing this because you play MMOs or sci fi games, you'll get a kick out of this, but I honestly cannot say how long that kick will last. 

But regardless, here's the main bullet points for good and bad, with some more detail below:
The good:
+ Multiple origins and hundreds of stories to play through from the outset. You can even pick 'alien' as a character, to make your own race, or to copy one from the series that isn't a listed option. I managed to create a Hirogen character to be my security officer with this.
+ Full character customisation that includes race, gender, look, class, outfit, including options to write your own backstory. As a general guideline, your classes can be compared to the following: Tactical = Soldier/warrior, Engineering = Tank/summoner, Scientist = Wizard/medic.
+ There are a huge variety of starships to play with, with their own customisation options and loadouts. These are not tied into your class either. You can be a scientist with a warship, or a tactical officer with an engineering powerhouse. These ships also reflect the aforementioned class comparisons, with science ships being very good at disabling enemy ships and supporting others, engineering vessels being tanky beasts that don't go down and tactical ships being far more aggressive, fighter-like gameplay.
+ You can get to maximum level (65) without paying a penny. There are microtransactions, but they are not necessary to progress. You get a new ship every 10 levels, up to 50, and the last free tier of ship (5 out of 6) can carry you through the story missions provided you keep your equipment up to date.
+ Creative narratives for each episode, sometimes supported with voice lines from the actual cast of the shows themselves! (shout out to Jeri Ryan and Kate Mulgrew in that area)
+ Creative designs for STO original ships and races, with some areas being outright gorgeous in their look and layout.

The bad:
- Microtransactions. While these are not necessary to play the game with, you will see options to buy everywhere. Additionally, other players in the TFOs (basically group missions) will fly ahead and decimate every enemy while you're still travelling to the mission, all because they spent money. Again, these are not necessary for a solo playthrough of the missions and stories, but you will definitely start to feel outclassed at level 50+.
- Repetitive gameplay. While this may be the case for a lot of MMOs, both space and ground missions feel rather repetitive, especially against spongy enemies in space. You fly around, tap the same skills every few seconds and wait for their HP bar to disappear. This isn't an issue to begin with, per say, but again something you notice shortly after getting your last free ship.
- Ground combat. The space combat, even with repetitiveness, is still pretty fun and smooth to play. Ground combat however, is not. It is slow and clunky, with weapons often not firing on the kill shots, melee characters interrupting their own animations and the fact that most ground combat looks like two opposite line ups of characters constantly pelting each other with small shots until one goes down. The one nice thing of this, is that for the most part, your character is joined by their crew on these missions, making them more than icons on your hotbar.

Overall, if you're a Star Trek fan, you've probably already decided to try this. For anyone else, I think this game is definitely worth a shot if you like sci fi and/or MMOs. The space controls for your ship are beautiful and it makes you truly feel like you're piloting one of Starfleet's ships. This is reflected in size too, as the galaxy class has next to no turning ability, compared to something like the defiant, which can zip around the map so much you'll get dizzy. I'll also point out that there's a fair bit of replayability too, by using the other character origins, up until the cardassian/mirror universe missions (usually the 7th set of missions on your list), giving you a unique experience each time. On a personal note, I can highly recommend the Romulan start as it's a really well thought out story of betrayal, revenge and pride.

Honestly though, with nearly 500 hours in it at this point, I can happily say that if any of this review has interested you, give this game a go! It's free after all! The development team are brilliant and constantly adding to the story and content with free updates, and you don't need to spend a penny to get a character to level 65. There is more here than you might expect in a game like this, so give it a go if you have the time.

[h1][i]“It's been a long road~”[/i] 🎵
~Diane Warren, Russell Watson[/h1]

Reviewing MMOs is a bad idea. Those games change so much on the way that reading the old reviews feels a lot like reading about entirely different game. Yet in this case? I think I'll make an exception. See, at this point the game doesn't change that much anymore. Publisher moved it to another developer, the one that is known to keep old MMOs alive, while instead of expansions, we've got new story episodes dropping now and then. Guess, it's a good time to look back at [b]STO[/b]. Lots of you, people, dislike [b]Enterprise[/b] opening, but let's just admit it – it's been a long road.

It all started almost 15 years ago, in 2010. It was about a year before [b]Star Wars: The Old Republic[/b], [b]The Lord of the Rings Online[/b] just went f2p... And here it was. A long-awaited game based on one of the most influential Sci-Fi shows in history. And you know what? It was pretty cool. [b]Cryptic[/b], creators of games like [b]City of Heroes[/b] and [b]Champions Online[/b], sure knew how to think outside the box. What did we get? Well, a lot of stuff, actually. The players were divided between two factions – [b]United Federation of Planets[/b] and [b]Klingon Defense Force[/b] (still are, while non-human and non-[b]Klingon[/b] chars simply join as allies), while gameplay revolves around two things – [b]WoW[/b]-like instances on ground and space combat.

In other words, we've got not one, but two games. The ground operations are our usual MMO stuff. Grab the gun, equip some skills and then kill things. The usual. Far from being bad, since some of such operations are pretty creative (a bit too creative at times if you know what I mean), but still, nothing special. Heck, some people prefer not to play ground missions at all and stick with... Yeah. You guessed it. The main dish. Space. [i]The final frontier.[/i]

The space battles in [b]STO[/b] is, exactly as it should be, a ship porn. There's a vast selection of ships in this game, both those from original media (shows, movies, books...), and exclusive to the game. And while usually, I'm not a fan of made up stuff, this time? I must say, those ships are great. So great there are actually collectible models with those. And I do have lots of them. Now think about it. Picking up your favorite [b]Star Trek[/b] ship, hiring a crew and then doing something I can somewhat compare to, say, [b]World of Tanks[/b] with 'em? Sounds like a dream, right? Well, in a way it is. [i]But[/i]. Only after a year on market, [b]STO[/b] followed [b]LoTRO[/b] into the f2p territory. And, as you can easily guess, all the best ships are sold separately now. Wait, wait, wait! Don't close this page yet, keep reading.

See, unlike most of the other f2p games, [b]STO[/b] actually has pretty nice f2p model. You [i]do[/i] earn premium currency with time (even more if you have more than one toon) and there's a never-ending cycle of giveaways and events that'll reward you with top tier ships. Which won't be as good as those that you'll pay for, of course, but still, those are pretty solid. In other words, the game is 100% playable for free. If you'll want to become top player, you'll still want to pay, say, the price of a [b]Final Fantasy XIV[/b], but that's it. That'll be enough for you to do PVP and stuff. And after that? After that you won't need to invest anything. One of the reasons I like this game. I mean, usually, f2p games are very hard on your wallet, while those that require subscription make me feel bad about literally burning money while not playing. This here? Is totally my kind of stuff. In a way, it feels a lot like “buy to play”. You buy some stuff to make one of them top builds and then forget about paying completely.

It's not that simple, though. The thing is, in its current form, [b]STO[/b] heavily revolves around dailies. So-called endeavors are a very long series of daily tasks that provide major bonuses to your stats account-wide. Nothing complicated, just kill some enemies here and do certain “instances” (called TFO) there. Usually takes about 30 minutes per day, but it means you'll need to be there. Every. Bloody. Day. Those events I've mentioned are like that too. Just be there. Otherwise even paying the real money won't help. I mean, what's the point paying for a good ship with the best hardware if you miss things like +50% damage from endeavors? And to complete your endeavors? You'll need to play for, like, a couple of years. Again, you won't need to invest lot of time. [b]STO[/b] is not one of those games that can ruin your personal life. But still, it's one of those games that you visit. Every day.

Even if you won't want to be a top player, though, [b]STO[/b] is a lot of fun. Why? Well, because of its story. It's smart (love it what they did with the [b]V'ger[/b] from the first movie), there's a lot of lore involved from all the shows, and the best of all? The story is voiced by real actors.  Lots and lots of our favorites are there – from [b]Leonard Nimoy[/b] ([b]Mr. Spock[/b]) to [b]Sonequa Martin-Green[/b] ([b]Michael Burnham[/b]). Even the passed actors are presented in a form of archive sound, while [b]Scotty[/b] is voiced by [b]James Doohan[/b]'s son, [b]Christopher[/b]. Same [b]Christopher[/b], who played [b]Scotty[/b] in that awesome fan series [b]Star Trek Continues[/b]. The other guys from [b]STC[/b] are here too, while story also brings back characters nobody expected to see again. Like, we all loved [b]Jadzia[/b] from [b]DS9[/b], but there was also something very special about [b]Ezri[/b], who showed us just how hard things can be for joined [b]Trill[/b]. It was a shame that she only had one season. Good news! [b]Nicole de Boer[/b] and her character is in [b]STO[/b] too. You like [b]Trek[/b]? You should totally play through story at least once. And you know what? It's free for everybody. No need to pay for the new episodes, no need to be a top player to clear the whole thing.

Sounds like a perfect MMO, right? Well... Not really. If something, [b]STO[/b] is far from perfection. It can be clunky, it's managed by ridiculously small team, which, instead of fixing ages old bugs, keep bringing the new ones in updates, cosmetics are half-broken and very hard to manage, while, the worst of all, there's no open world areas. Well, technically, those exist, but they just... don't feel right. Galaxy map is empty and useless ([b]Cryptic[/b] tried to fix that by adding encounters and mini operations called “patrols” for different systems, but all in all, it didn't help and exploring just isn't a thing), while so-called battlezones are painfully repetitive and, most likely, you'll only be doing those for endeavors. And it's a [i]huge[/i] problem. Summer / winter festivals, where lots of people gather on special locations show exactly how much fun this game can be with proper open world environment, but no. It is not a thing.

[b]STO[/b] is just that. A game you visit every day for 30-60 minutes, clear endeavors, do a couple of favorite TFOs and then quit because there's nothing else to do (if you finished story that is). That's probably why the majority of players here are old alcoholics who keep whining about how bad the “new [b]Trek[/b]” is. Don't get me wrong, the audience here is far from being toxic as in, say, [b]WoW[/b], but still, “I'm so drunk”, “[b]Discovery[/b] is the worst!” and “Let's talk politics” is what zone chat is all about. You have been warned. In other words, you want MMO experience with a huge world and lots of things to do? This here is not it. Technically, there's [i]a lot[/i] of things here, but at this point most of those don't matter (even transwarp feature can be ignored by simply utilizing new “jump to an episode” option). And in a way? It's a good thing. With a fair monetization policy and with no need to invest too much time? [b]STO[/b] is, like, perfect addition to your [b]Star Trek[/b] experience. Dixi.

For all its foibles--which are many--this game offers something I haven't seen in a long time.

It actually feels like Star Trek.

Star Trek is optimistic, that's part of the appeal. It posits a world better than our own, a vision of what humanity could be if we have the time and technology to achieve it.

Unfortunately, Trek has gone through an interminably long phase of constantly becoming Darker and Edgier. In the process, it lost what made it special, becoming just another grimdark science fiction dystopia with Hard People making Hard Choices. Even Picard, which (eventually) started trying to reconstruct Star Trek, still features starships that are almost unlit for no reason beyond "we want to make a darker, edgier appearance." Much of this can be traced back to DS9 and VOY playing with the formula, and later folks making the classic mistake of confusing violence, cynicism, and trauma for depth, maturity, and drama, a perennial fault of our age. I got so tired of the "everything must always be (grim)dark all the time" that I just disengaged from Star Trek entirely.

STO has changed that.

Now, although I don't always care for the writing, and the mechanics are pretty clearly P2W at least nowadays (no idea what it was like in the past), I value STO because it's the first time I've felt like I'm actually getting Trek content in the past 15 years that has the original spirit. It's hopeful. Terrible things sometimes happen, but we do our best to pick ourselves back up. Sometimes, people are bastards, but those who are willing to do the hard work to build a better future CAN succeed. We don't need to become horrific monsters in order to protect ourselves. Ingenuity, compassion, and tenacity can truly save the day, at least in the end, though we may pay a high price to get there. Etc.

If you loved the spirit of Trek that TOS and TNG articulated, that DS9 and VOY questioned but ultimately respected, then you'll get something positive out of STO's story. For that reason alone, it's worth playing. Just...try to avoid thinking too much about the damn pay-to-win. You don't need to spend money to play, and enjoy, the story. The only reason I spent any money at all was so I could play a Caitian, 'cause I like cat-people. If you can convince a friend or two to play with you, you can get through basically all content without any real issue.

The Pros: If you're a star trek fan you're going to have a blast playing this game right up to a certain point. The story missions are genuine episodes of Star Trek pulled from the expanded universe. My favorite mission is, of course, Quarks Lucky Seven where you have to steal back the sword of Kahless from the Iconians, and there are a lot of missions to play. The game play is fun, the mechanics aren't that difficult to understand, and the early gearing system is pretty good. You're going to be playing both star ship battles and away team missions. Not only are there a lot of missions there are different factions you can play all with their own vanilla story. Vanilla story meaning all the faction stories merge after a certain point. 

The Cons: Remember I mention that "up to a certain point" comment? That's going to be end game content. Grinding for mats, joining a fleet, and spending real money for certain items like T6 star ships are going to be an absolute must. You are going to have to do some pretty hard research on YouTube and forum sites into how to do a proper build for both your ground crew and star ships for end game content and you better believe those builds absolutely involve spending real money, and the not spending real money "method" is so uber tedious it will take you years to grind the mats necessary. The meta builds are always changing and a lot of the critical mats are severely time gated and can't even be overturned by spending real money, dilithium to be specific. Trying to understand what makes a good build effective requires some serious nerd power in breaking down meta data into spreadsheets and working the different variables in gear combinations vs. the specific content you're playing. Yes, you read that right, you are going to need different builds for different content that require different gear that will cost money. So before you spend a dime you better know what you're doing in your build or you might just waste 20 dollars on an in game currency to purchase a piece of gear you don't even need or worse was from 2 expansions ago. 

My Honest Opinion: Play this game for the story and stay far away from the end game content.

I've been playing this game on and off for 12 years now, and accounting for the time I've played before I had it tied to Steam, I've probably put 1000+ h into it. If you like Star Trek, you will like this game. With a narrative that incorporates the pre-existing lore and takes it into a direction that is, despite being an alternate timeline from the shows, still very much believable as a Star Trek universe. So much has been faithfully transferred, and plenty of the original cast has taken up some of their roles as voice actors here. There are also plenty of options for customization for both your captain, ship and crew. There are also deep mechanics to explore when it comes to outfitting your ship and crew, but if you just want to play it for the story or just enjoy role-playing, it's easy to get through, even without giving it much thought or grinding. Minmaxing only really matters if you want to play against other players or enjoy it in the first place.
It's not perfect, obviously. The game is over ten years old, and the graphics reflect that, and there are some quirks in the engine that make it feel less smooth than a modern game. If that is a big turn-off for you, then that might be it, but I've always found the story and setting compelling enough to overlook it, and even with the engine they have, they do put a lot work and attention to detail in where it counts. Also, while the game is free to play, you have to pay to unlock certain ships, more room in your inventory and bank, more slots for bridge officers for your crew (although you technically don't need more than the game gives you from the start) etc., and yes, there's lockboxes/gatcha. You mostly don't have to spend money to get a lot of this stuff, there are other ways to get them, but they involve a lot of grinding. Although, with the amount of stuff you can do for free, I don't think it's fair to fault the devs for having to have a way to earn money. I have spent money on the game, but never opened a lootbox, and I've had a great time with what I've gotten for it, especially because most things can be caught on sale regularly. The game is also only pay to win in the sense that if you're really chasing for the highest DPS, spending money is probably necessary, but if you just want to RP or play the story, there is really no need. Most of the classic hero ships can be gotten through the regular story - the Intrepid, Galaxy, Constitution classes etc.
In the end, if you're a Trek fan, I can only recommend you at least give it a shot, create a character, and give the first few missions a spin. The later missions have more of the original cast, but if you begin as a TOS Federation character, you'll meet a lot of familiar faces from TOS right away (and even some more recent ones ;), and have a normal Federation character after the first story arc, with which you can play through all the entire rest of the story.

Be careful with this game. It is, fundamentally, a good game. The stories are incredible and voluminous after 15 years of development and writing. It's well structured to suck you into an online world of Star Trek that is deep and engaging. The new owners, DECA, are responsive to the players and seem to be competent in addressing issues. There are moments in this game, even now, after all this time, that take my breath away.

Here comes the but...

It is rapaciously, avariciously monetized on a scale that would make a Ferengi blush with embarrassment. The lockbox and acquisition mechanics are designed to be addictive and predatory. The value of what you'd need to break into ingame (elite) content *starts* at around $300 USD. DPS chasers spend thousands. The most efficient grind rate I've been able to achieve to harvest these resources (dilithium and energy credits) works out to be about $.75 an hour, and that's after weeks of grinding to even get to where you can do that (admiralty system access, enough ships in your fleet, etc.). Moreover, to do this at scale (as in more than $.26 per day), you'll need multiple characters combining resources.

Do you *need* to run elite content to enjoy this game? Certainly not. Can you enjoy this game fully in F2P mode? Absolutely. But I don't know anyone who has. You need to understand that you'll be jumping into task force operations where whales are absolutely obliterating the enemy in seconds. You won't even know why. There are lockboxes, annual bundle sales that run north of $100 USD, and the infamous Mudd's market. If (when) you must buy something, wait for a zen charge bonus to buy the zen, and only buy the item on sale.

If you're prepared to deal with this level of monetization, then you'll find STO to be a very full, engaging, and enjoyable experience.

I've played this game since being a beta tester and while I do still enjoy it; you should have realistic expectations. As the only Star Trek game this gives it a big plus but often it rides on this very notion. This game could have been so much more but it is effectively a smash em up style MMO exactly the same as CO and NWN in terms of the gameplay. What we hoped for all those years ago was a refined tactical shooter; what we have presently is a combat game that is explosive to the point of it being OTT. 

My biggest gripes with STO are:
- Lack of ability to retain builds fully; the tedious detail you have to go into to switch between a build, or even a ship. You cannot save your skill points you have to spend money to respec them if you move from one ship type to another. Then you have your duty officers and traits on top to manually tweak to get the most out of your new choice of ship.

- Combat Gameplay: It's too erratic; not at all like the tactical shooting we see in Star Trek. Shield vectors matter little, this is effectively press space bar and unleash everything at once. Ground combat is also drawn out, and not even remotely fun.

- Things to do: I really wish the game had more going for it but after a while you're just logging in to see what new ships there are.

- Pay wall - So many ships are hidden behind a pay wall of some sort; a real shame that they don't allow players to access ships through ingame credits. 

I would love to see this game evolve into something it deserved to be.

Overall this is a fun game. There are problems aplenty and I can absolutely understand why someone would be unwilling to participate because of those problems. But, for those of us with some degree of personal control there's also a good deal of fun game here. 14 years of fairly regular updates have left a huge amount of story to play through and enjoy even on a totally free account, and the game's difficulty is low enough that running through the game solo isn't an issue. But, it wouldn't be honest or fair to just blindly praise the game.

Cons:
- Loot Boxes: The game uses Infinity Lock Boxes (and sometimes limited time event lock boxes) which drop from enemies frequently and can be obtained from the in game store for free, but require keys to be opened which must be purchased. These Lock Boxes have incredibly poor odds (less than 5% drop rate on the Grand Prize with effectively zero pity) and even if you're lucky enough to get the grand prize it will only unlock that item for one character on your account.
- Microtransactions: The main real money store front (the Zen Store, sometimes still called the C-Store) will offer a large number of unlockable and consumable items, many of which are not cosmetic. These also range wildly in price from a few dollars to hundreds of dollars.
- Grind: Not as bad as some, but as this is a Free To Play game the devs will have events frequently and sometimes overlapping to maintain interest. These are optional and generally do reward good things but that is a drain on your time. This game will ask for a lot of your time, an hour or so each day for focused players.
- Bugs: While the game is still being fixed and updated constantly (weekly updates), there are still a large number of long standing issues that have yet to be addressed. The team is clearly working on these bugs, even squashing a big one not that long ago (bad binary file causing certain levels to be impossible to complete), but it's not a completely clean situation. This is no Bethesda game, just some unpleasantness from time to time.
- Stability: While the servers are largely fine, this is an old game with a smaller player base. The servers just don't hold up well to peak hours. This becomes considerably more of a problem at higher difficulty levels when skills don't register being used or server latency starts moving you around the map.

Pros:
- Lots to do: At the time of writing the game is 14 years old with an insane amount of content added over the years. If you have the time to spend or just want to work through the main story and ignore everything else, several full priced games can't compete with the amount of content available here. Get involved with a Fleet (STO's guild system) for ways to spend in game currencies for more rewards including some of the best ships in the game.
- Real World Money is Optional: While there is a PvP scene, it is by no means the main draw for the game. Coupled with the relatively low difficulty level, this means that you really don't need any of those fancy ships in the cash shop. You can get by just fine with the stuff they give you for free. And multiple times a year there will be events to just earn higher power ships and gear. This goes doubly so for the Lock Boxes, none of that is required to just play the game. Most isn't even really valuable until you're getting into Advanced or Elite content.
- Gameplay: While the ground combat isn't good for a variety of reasons, the space combat is tons of fun. Kitting our your star ship with weapons and other gear then boat racing around while blasting enemies never gets old. The game is pretty close to classless, with the class only adding to a pool of open ended skills. This means build variety is basically endless, even on a single character.
- Customization: Paradox came to STO after they built Champions Online, which came after they made City of Heroes. And they used that knowledge to make what I still consider to be one of the best character generators in the industry. It's tempered by the limits of "Star Trek Character", but the Alien species type available to most factions will allow a considerable amount of visual variety. I've seen near perfect recreations of Star Trek cast members standing along side Invader Zim.
- The devs actually like Star Trek: If it's been in Star Trek, in any of the shows or movies, it's likely somewhere in this game. Be it a ship, a weapon, some mcguffin on some world somewhere, an unlockable dance on a certain world, it's here somewhere. Sadly, a lot of that is locked behind loot boxes, but a huge amount of it is just free if you go looking for it. But, with enough dedication and maybe some luck, if you have a specific Star Trek fantasy? You're probably going to be able to live it out in this game. Plus, the staff often gets the actual actors to reprise their roles as VAs in the game. Leonard Nimoy narrates the early game for Federation players, and congratulates them on leveling up. Nana Visitor interacts with Rene Auberjonois. Denise Crosby returns constantly. There's even a monument in every major faction hub remembering the talents we've lost along the way. Old and New Trek alike, this game holds it all dear.
- Buying the premium currency is optional: It is possible to exchange Refined Dilithium (a currency earned in game) for Zen (cash shop premium currency). The exchange rate is not great (500 Dil to 1 Zen), but it's possible to do and handled entirely in game. So, with enough patience and dedication, even a free to play player can get the really cool ships from the cash shop. Even the mega expensive $500 bundles.

I'd like to believe that the pros outweigh the cons, but those are some pretty big cons. And it's hard to say what the future for the game will be, but I'd like to believe that Deca has good intentions. I'd say the game is worth trying out. Can't beat the startup price.

This game has something for all fans of Star Trek. While the bulk of it might reference The Original Series, The Next Generation and it's spin-offs and Enterprise, there are definitely elements of the newer installations of Star Trek whether you as the fan, love it, hate it, or somewhere in between.

I will warn anyone considering to play this, that depending on how you game, this game can be difficult to learn without the proper guidance or research. While the in-game store makes it look like it's absolutely pay-to-win, it isn't.  However, the player can grind to achieve better builds for their ships if they decide to buy the latest Tier 6 ship, or stick with their free Tier 5 upon reaching level 61. It seems the PvP in this game died, but the PvE Task Force Operations are alive and well.

There are some glaring bugs that never got addressed, like the changeling in the "Jabberwocky" mission, the target in one of the Klingon missions for Klingon recruits (active during the KDF recruitment periods), and probably others as well. Depending on how your perception is, this may or may not turn you away from this game. Still, however, life persists in this game, and the community is live and well. Many things have changed over the years with Star Trek Online and unfortunately, I cannot share any experience to compare what type of game Star Trek Online was to the one of today. Be prepared to die a lot depending on your missions. If you're a masochist like me, but love Star Trek, then this game just might be for you.

As with many games, this one also comes with problems on top of bugs. As all die-hard Trekkies know, it should be possible to cross-faction or team up with different factions in this game, as cooperation is the foundation of the United Federation of Planets. Clearly, it isn't possible. Sure, if you want to play a Federation Klingon, you have to pay to unlock the option, but you cannot play a Klingon teaming up with a seemingly honorable Starfleet warrior or play a Starfleet Vucan who knows that it's logical to team up with Klingon Empire aligned people to face bigger threats, because that's the basis of Infinite Diversity in Infinite Combinations.

The space battles is where it's at in this game. If you pay attention to the detail of each ship and the writing, you can tell that the people who put time into this game love Star Trek, despite it's problems. At least, I can attest that this game is playable. If you want something fast-paced and something you don't want to put money into or a lot of time (or a bit of both), then this is not the game for you.

I've played a number from MMO's from LotRo, ESO, Rift, and SWO and yet none has kept me logging in daily quite like STO has. And the weird thing is that I am not a huge Trekkie either, or should I say I wasn't a huge trekkie before I started. LotR and ES have both had me investing far more time in the past in other games and delving into their lore, but I started playing STO about 3 years ago simply because I started rewatching next generation. 

Star Trek Online is very easy to play in bitesize chunks because of the episodic nature of the chapters and missions, and honestly it is done in a way that no other MMO I have played has ever beaten. In games like LotrO and ESO I found myself logging in after a week away or an extended absence and simply having no idea which quests I was doing or why and so would generally drop them all and start picking up random quests until I found a common story thread to follow. It's not a major issue, but it is a bit jarring when going back to a game after a break. With STO though, the chapters just seem to be more neatly wrapped up and easier to digest and there is a very definite order where you just follow one by one when it comes to the main story. There are other world missions that you pick up on the way too, but are generally repeatable which means they don't tend to affect the main story much. I don't know why but STO just feels neater when it comes to storytelling, and it really helps you not feel overwhelmed. 

The devs also keep constant mini events running where you can earn ships, upgrades and in game items on pretty much a monthly basis which in my view also makes it one of the most generous MMO's I have played. Most games give a daily reward for free, but its usually a one use consumable or something you never would have bought anyway. In this game, the ships alone are worth logging in for the events as each one can be claimed on every character and every ship has a unique trait or sometimes equipment that can help you experiment with builds. I see a lot of "STO is pay to win" but in my experience that just isn't true. They are more than generous with free stuff and they have regular sales on the in game store. Most of what people cry about the cost of seems to be things like rare ships too, which just seems to me like a huge FOMO that they themselves need to either cough up or get over. You can absolutely play this game without investing much at all, as I played f2p for quite a while before starting to spend money on it. 

As well as the in game rewards and freebies, there are regular update giveways on sites like intel, alienware and Steel series and these giveaways tend to have something that ties into the latest game update. For example a recent update was all about the borg and so the giveaways had borg consoles and borg ground weapons that you could claim. What is more every single time they do these giveaways, every one contains a pack that gives you bank and inventory space which means that there is another thing you don't necessarily have to buy in game. These sites always have their own unique updates too giving away different items, and so at each update you get to claim 2-4 different ones and so that is 2-4 different bank and inventory packs. Again, in my opinion just another showing of how overly generous the game actually is. 

There are also in game work arounds to some of the paid content, for example one thing people buy is "cross faction flying" but this can be unlocked for free just by levelling a Klingon KDF character to max level. Once your klingon is max level, every character on the account can fly whatever ship they like so again saves you money after a little time investment. 

As for levelling too, I find this to be one of the easiest games to level characters in personally. I have something like 8 max level characters and most of them I haven't really played that much. They have been levelled mainly through events, random TFO's (group missions) and solo patrols. This wasn't for any other reason than because I wanted different characters of different races to be able to jump in and play when I felt like it and have access to similar skills across them. 

Quite honestly, even as a someone who is fairly new to star trek I can say that this game gives you a lot to log in for and a lot of content to play. It also got me interested in watching other star trek shows such as Deep Space 9 and TOS, neither of which ever interested me before. The fact that the game hires many of the voice actors to reprise their roles got me wanting to know more about them and so it kindled a bit of a star trek deep dive and in turn made me appreciate the whole fandom a lot more. 

My final thought is simply that if you are on the fence about trying this game, just try it. I was and I did, and I haven't looked back.

This is a Star Trek theme park.  If you're okay with that, you'll probably enjoy yourself.  It's nice hearing Armin Shimmerman and Tim Russ (among many, many Trek alumni) reprise their roles, and the space combat is a lot of fun.  I can even say from experience you can get by with the free ships for the majority of the content, and you can do Advanced content without spending money, though you will need to be on top of your piloting game (and you are guaranteed three free endgame-tier ships a year.  They may not necessarily be great, but they're good enough for Advanced team content, which is what the majority play).  The graphics aren't bad for an early 2010s MMO,  though endgame space and ground combat can get very visually noisy.  The audio is also a treat, with new sounds to go with classic ones (Prophets help you if someone's rocking 23rd Century Phasers.  That *FWEE* is still as ear-piercing as it was in the 1960s.) and music that ranges from serviceable to above-average.  

Ground combat is fairly dull, unfortunately, though it's not hard to make yourself overpowered enough to make it a non-factor.  There's also a lot of grinding at endgame, with multiple "Reputations" to work through that can only be advanced from currency earned from specific queued or open-world missions.  While you can only earn so much reputation a day, you can easily work on several at once.  

The game does, however, "ask" a lot of money.  Tier 6 ships (which are what just about everyone flies) all come with special traits that you can then use on any other ship your character has.  These ships cost $30USD, which is about what a good indie title goes for.  And if you want to fly one of the numerous one-off alien ships instead of the ones for your faction, you're going to be spending your real money on keys to open lockboxes or trying to play the in-game Exchange for one.  Fortunately, the game often runs "recruit" events that let you earn powerful gear for that character as well as bonuses for your account that can make the grind more tolerable.  

So, this is a yes with caveats.  If you find an active Fleet to join, you can stomach ground stuff, and if you have enough self-control not to whale, you can have a good time.  Otherwise, try watching someone play it on Youtube to gauge if you want to jump in.  If you're just looking for a space game to mess with spaceship stuff, I'd look elsewhere, like Starsector.

I have been playing STO for several years now. From there I asked a steady stream of questions and got very useful advice on in-game economy, earning upgrade kits, and similar topics.  
My advice to new players is to ask many questions and not be afraid to ask for help.  There are a number of details that are not even mentioned in the tutorials, but despite the never-ending stream of political bad takes in the big chat hubs there are even more decent folk who will take advise a newcomer.

The real goal of STO is, of course, "Space Barbie."  Dressing your crew toons in stylish uniforms or casual wear is amusing, but the bigger draw is the starship selection.  The game IS free-to-play, and the normal level grind will give you several opportunities to earn your choice of basic ships appropriate to the Federation, Romulan, or Klingon career paths.  Additionally, there are summer and winter events in which one can earn a free ship as well as useful personal gear.
Unfortunately for people without trust funds, the most coveted ships and gear are not free.  The in-game store has a decent sale from time to time but it is clear that your money is supposed to be theirs.  I kept to the ftp ethos for years but finally decided that a purchase now and then was not fatal.  To be clear, it is a luxury, not a necessity.  If something I really wanted came along, I would buy it only if I could do without a corresponding purchase elsewhere.  Most often that meant not buying beer for a little while, so we're not talking really large sums.  

Sadly, I can no longer make purchases because Arc decided I have to go through them.  I hope they enjoy not having that little bit of revenue stream any longer.

I've played this game a little bit since I found it a couple of months ago, and I have a couple things to say:

First and foremost, a lot of the negative reviews on here focus on endgame gameplay: the sometimes ridiculous microtransactions, how long the grind to get new high level ships is, or the fact that new missions and continuations to the storyline take a seemingly unjustified long amount of time to come out. And while all of those things are certainly true, it doesn't really become an issue for new players for a long time. If you take your time just playing through all the storylines, you'll easily get a hundred hours of gameplay minimum before even having to worry about any of that stuff. And by then you don't even have to keep playing if they become huge issues for you.

The most enjoyable part of the game (at least for me) is the story. All of the arcs have their moments, even the ones that pale in comparison to others. In addition to that, there's also many incredibly complex game systems that have surprised me in how much you can do with them. They'll get introduced gradually as you level up, and it can be a bit overwhelming at first, but just remember you don't have to start diving into each system as soon as you can access it.

The graphics aren't the best you'll see, but I'd argue this adds to the already amazing immersion of commanding a starship in the Star Trek universe, as the grand majority of Star Trek shows don't have the best effects by today's standards either. There are some bugs in the game as well, but they haven't been majorly gamebreaking in my experience. In fact, it's surprising well-maintained for a fourteen year-old game.

Overall, if you like Star Trek, get this game and at least play through the majority of the story (it is free, after all) - after that you can decide whether or not to keep playing and go into the endgame.

I recommend this MMO because you can really play it for free. There will be some grind walls, but nothing too serious.
The game offers a lot of PvE content: story missions, co-op actions, and big zones on some planets.
The story is quite long, and they still regularly add new episodes. Which is quite a surprising thing to see in MMO, since you run it mostly for the story, and unlikely to run it again.

The game also features a lot of ships and other content from the Star Trek universe. Even if you're not a fan, it's still quite interesting because of variety.

Now for the cons.
The graphics is dated, everything is arcadey, forget about PvP, and they always try to sell you lootboxes and other premium stuff with ads on loading screens, events and daily tasks. In other words, all the stuff from junk MMOs, except you can play it for free with no catch.
Yes, this game was never a serious thing. I remember we laugh at its beta on EVE Online forums, the graphics was kinda old from the start (they're updating it though). And theres so much of it, its hard to recommend this game. Storyline missions are ruined by it and I sigh every time I'm forced to do it just to progress the story. You'd think by now, after 14 grueling years of it, they'd listen to the feedback and get rid of it, or at the very least reduce it if they're not going to fix it. Please, for the love of god, do something, its a huge blemish on what is otherwise a great game.

Good MMO in a sea of shite, it's a Whale's paradise but still very F2P friendly. 

Star Trek Online is made with love and passion from the developers, they've got the original actors from the TV shows to reprise their roles and voice act in well written story. There are plenty of story arc for the players to play through and explore more of the Star Trek universe. Most of them are written very well and kept interesting enough to hold the players' attention at all times. 

You gotta love this game's music, the main character selection screen has got the BEST background music ever. I have looped the game in the background over the years just for the music. 

The graphics has not aged well, you can see that most evidently on ground where the textures are disgustingly bad to the human eye. However, an advantage of low resolution texture is the extreme fast loading times between areas. It takes no more than 30 seconds for me to load from one area to the next.

Now, combat in this game is unlike anything you've played. Space combat where you pilot your starship is one of the best PvE combat system in anything similar. you can move in a 3D environment (3 axies XYZ) and position your ship for a broadside barrage of lasers. Your starship can be further customised with different weapons and loadouts to varied styles. It's glorious, Beam Boats to Cannon Volleys and Torpedoes build.

Now for what you have waited for. Is the game P2W?

Yes. Like all MMOs, STO has been alive for 14 years. You don't have a MMO running for 14 years without massive player's whaling. Most of the best DPS consoles and traits(captain and ship) in the game are obtained from Lockboxes(Lootbox) or from Zen Store ships.

Fortunately for you F2Ps, it is not all lost. You can reach very competitive DPS numbers by just spending time in the game and reaching Lvl 50 to unlock the Reputation system which has BiS gear for free. Some of the story mission also award you with very good end game scalable gear. Every story basically give enough for 1 level up each time, so you can reach max level (65) in a few days if you grind long.

This game is still good, you're be joining a friendly and knowledgeable community. Besides, this is the ONLY good Star Trek game out there.

First, let me say that while i've only played this around 8 hours on Steam, I actually bought this game when it released more than a decade ago. I had played to maximum level back then, and watched the game decline from a monthly subscription game into a mobile-like money sucking free to play game.

So the first complaint I have about this game is its "free to play" nature. Like all games that claim to be free to play, there is a real money store integrated into the UI and it is basically where you purchase anything beyond the most absolute basics. This goes far, far beyond just being a cosmetic shop, it actually locks the overwhelming majority of ships, playable species, and bridge officer species behind a pay wall. You can technically play for free, but only playing basic races like humans, andorians, and a couple of others. As far as ships go, you're restricted to the free to play ships which there is basically 1 for each career path every 10 levels and the highest freebie ship I believe is tier 4, while the highest possible is tier 6.

Not only that, but the ships you buy with real money include special equipment and consoles that are very powerful and basically encourages you to buy entire ships just for access to the one specific piece of equipment it has so you can use all of these items together on your preferred ship. This is a pay to win tactic. You not only have to buy the best ship you can afford, but also have to buy other ships you may not even want if you want to be competitive with other players.

The worst part about it though is that all of these ships show up in the basic ship store, where free to play players go to purchase their ships. This means that when its time to upgrade your free to play ship to the next one, you have to go through this very long list of ships you have no access to and cannot buy before you finally get to the bottom of the list where the free ones are. It is also not immediately clear which ships you can and cannot purchase because there are like 3 different currencies, as well as random other items, needed to buy them. The whole system can be intensely confusing for new players.

My next gripe about the game is that everything feels extremely dated. Even when this game originally released back in 2010, the graphics and animations were rather subpar for the time, and in the decade + since then, they apparently haven't change any of it. Maybe the ships in space might look a bit better, they do look pretty clean, but all of the actual characters and away mission settings and maps look like something you would see from a game from 2005. I typically don't care a whole lot about graphics in games, but in this one it irks me particularly because you are required by the gameplay to spend so much time doing away missions. Everything is very awkwardly scaled with things like ship interior hallways being 20 feet wide, the bridges being 3 times larger than they should be and filled mostly with empty space. Away missions are almost universally linear in design where you basically just go in a straight line down hallways or pathways on planets with absolutely no ability to actually explore the area and there is nothing to see down there anyway but invisible walls.

Every mission follows the exact same formula. You fly up to a planet, usually destroy a handful of alien ships, press F near some random macguffins (typically satellites that need reprogramming or anomalies that need scanning or whatever, but you just move close and press F for everything), then beam to the planet or space station where you kill a handful of stationary pre-spawned enemies, press F on a few more items or people, then usually fight a few waves of enemies that spawn and rush at you. Every single mission plays out this way, these are the only elements of the game that exist. Then you beam back to your ship, and the mission is either over or sometimes you have to destroy a couple more ships, then its done.

It can be kind of fun, but it gets intensely repetitive very, very quickly. It's like they took the most mundane and boring aspects of a MMO and turned that into the only gameplay loop in the whole game. Feels like nothing but kill/fetch quests repeating indefinitely. Also, given that you flat out KILL all enemies in every mission and blow up multiple ships, your federation ship basically kills thousands of people every single mission which feels intensely unfederationlike.

On the plus side, I always enjoyed the customization of your bridge officers. You can make them look however you want, name them whatever you want, and change the powers they use both in space combat and as away team members. I always found that aspect to be neat, even though in reality most powers are rather useless and there are definitely optimal ways to set them up. Away teams were also unique in the sense that you and your bridge officers make up your own 5 person party, like most MMOs, except the other 4 characters are NPCs you control. So you can make a tank character, a healer character, and DPS characters to accompany you on away missions without relying on other players, and I did always think that was very cool.

But again, after the game went free to play they kind of fucked it all up because back when you payed $10 a month to play the game, EVERYTHING in game used Energy Credits as the currency. You could use that to buy officers, to change officer skills, to buy ships, to buy equipment, to do literally everything. Now that its "free to play" there are 3 different currencies shoehorned in to try to get you to spend real money to acquire anything. Now you have to figure out which currency you need for each thing and try to obtain it.

It is technically possibly to acquire the other currencies without paying any money, but it takes an absurd amount of time and is very convoluted. For example, you acquire the "Dilithium" resource in small amounts when completing missions. You can then refine it into "Refined Dilithium" but you can only convert a certain amount each day to put an artificial cap on the rate you can acquire it. Some things cost Refined Dilithium, but most of the things cost their "Zen Bucks" currency or whatever it is, and you can exchange Refined Dilithium for Zen Bucks at a horrible rate.

So you're basically looking at doing a handful of missions to get enough dilithium to convert the max amount in a single day, then you convert it. Repeat this process until you reach the maximum possible amount of refined dilithium you can acquire, then you trade ALL of it for a SINGLE zen buck. The ships usually cost something like 10,000 zen bucks. So you'd have to do that 10,000 times. It would take literally years to acquire a single ship for free. Absolute madness.

I think the game was alright back when it launched, but all the pay to win crap they added over the years made it horrific.

If you're a big fan of star trek, it might be worth getting to play sparingly. It can potentially be fun in very short bursts, but it is so intensely repetitive that really the only thing that ever changes are the types of ships you are blowing up and those are more or less randomized, no real sense of progression there. But you have to endure a lot of very dated mechanics and UI elements to play the game which makes it very unappealing as well.

I think if they remade this game from the ground up with better graphics, modern UI design, and remove all the pay to win nonsense, it could potentially be fun, but right now its a mildly amusing distraction from time to time at best and a complete waste of time at worst.
