[b]New York Style Pizza[/b]

14 g instant yeast
617g water - 95F
950g all-purpose flour
19g fine sea salt
25g granulated sugar
American Pizza Sauce and Toppings:
1 tablespoon (14g) butter
1 tablespoon (9g) extra virgin olive oil
6 cloves garlic, rough chopped
2 teaspoons (4g) red pepper flakes
28 oz (794g) can of crushed tomato
2 teaspoons (2g) dried oregano
1.5 tablespoons (21g) granulated sugar
salt and pepper to taste
Splash of olive oil
2 cups (227g) low moisture mozzarella, fresh grated
2 cups (200g) Monterey jack cheese, fresh grated
1/2 cup (26g) parmigiano reggiano, fresh grated

[u]Pizza Dough:[/u]

Preheat the oven and a baking steel or pizza stone at 500F for 45 minutes before utilizing it.

Whisk yeast and sugar into your water, and allow it to sit for 5 minutes. In a separate bowl, add flour and salt and mix by hand to combine. Pour your water mixture into your flour and mix by hand until you get a rough dough, then transfer to a work surface and knead until it starts to pull away from the work surface and is relatively smooth.

Place your dough in a greased bowl, then cover with plastic wrap and let rise for 1 - 2 hours at room temperature or until double in size.

Punch down your dough and dive into 300g pieces. Form those pieces into balls and place them in a floured proofing pizza box, cover with a lid, and proof at room temperature for 3 - 4 hours. (If you do not have a proofing pizza box, you can use a floured baking sheet, cover it with an inverted baking sheet and wrap it in plastic wrap.)

[u]American Pizza Sauce and Toppings:[/u]

In a medium sauce pot, add butter and olive oil. Set that over medium-high heat; once the butter melts add garlic, cook until fragrant, add pepper flakes, and cook, stirring occasionally, until the garlic begins to brown on the edges.
Add crushed tomatoes, oregano, salt, and a splotch of olive oil, boil over medium-high, reduce heat to low, and simmer for 12 minutes, stirring occasionally or until thickened and viscous—season with salt to taste and let it cool down.

[u]Assembly:[/u]

Place one of your pizza doughs onto a floured pizza peel, and flour your dough generously.

Punch your dough down in the center, working your way out to create a ¼” wide. Pick up your dough, place it over your closed fists, and rotate it around, gently stretching to 13” to 14”.

Place a couple of spoons of your sauce, starting in the center, spreading in little circles, and working your way to the edge until it gets evenly spread out.

In a medium-size mixing bowl, place mozzarella cheese, Monterey Jack, and Parmigiano; mix until combined. Sprinkle your cheese mixture to your desire and place in the oven onto your baking steel and bake for 5 - 7 minutes or until the edge gets golden brown and the cheese melts.

Lots of [i] missions [/i] were just cluttered with 30+ enemies and the combat isn't much fun truthfully, especially the space flight. All the enemies outside of the first 5-10 minutes were insectoid - oh god, how original! As if there's not enough games with bugs in them.  

Seeing characters like Odo and other from DS9, etc, is pretty cool. 

The graphics are KOTOR level of fine I guess. I'm not fussy over graphics much. 

So I only actually played a few hours maybe but that was enough time to assess the basics like combat and space flight, etc, and I didn't feel like continuing. 

Now I'm not at all obsessed with Star Trek (only ever watched TOS, DS9 and some of the motion pictures in their entirety and couldn't stomach the rest) so that also plays a part in my decision. 

I would say 100% if you're simply looking for an MMO to play, just look again. WoW, ESO, SWTOR or hell, even Age of Conan (it's slightly more tolerable). Maybe Fallout 76 or Black Desert Online. If you value your sanity, you will heed my warning and never look in the direction of this game as long as you live.

That said, the reasons I don't recommend this game are as follows (these obviously contribute to my opinion.  Not everyone would give these the same weight, or maybe even consider them as actually being negatives.  But they are to me):

1) Bugs.  There are quite a few of them.  Game breaking ones are rare to encounter, but ones that cause a level of frustration are a bit more common.  Even some new content doesn't even work correctly out of the box in their very primary function (which you would have thought had been thoroughly tested).  But that's not really the worst part of it... it's the fact that many of them are allowed to persist.  Months go by, sometimes years without a fix.  And I get that this happens with every game to some extent, but of the ones I've played, this one is worse than others (not saying it is the worst, just bad enough to be worth pointing out).  There are even entire zones of content that haven't worked right since their release 7 years ago.  No one bothers with these areas anymore because of it.  And the responses to these things?  "We'll fix it when we have the time" or "We don't have anyone left working here that knows that section of code".  They're too focused on releasing new content (cause that's their money earner).

2) End game provides no challenge and isn't very fun or engaging.  Putting aside the fact that you can hit max level with ease (by the time you're half way through the story content), once you're there and take some time to level up your gear, there's nothing left that provides much of a challenge.  The only things preventing you from soloing it all (including team focused content) are via spreading things out so you literally couldn't cover everything by yourself, or by introducing cheap gimmicks that gate your progression (boss is down to half health... activate the immunity which can only be disabled via these other means).  This didn't used to be the case.  Back in 2012-2013 when I first used to play, none of this was possible and you actually had to work with a team of people to take down bosses.  Power creep, though, has come a long way, while all the content in the game (including newly released stuff) stays at the same difficulty.  So, again, while it's fun to to play up through, that's where it ends.  After that, it holds no challenge, nothing to keep you engaged.  You just park, buff up, fire, 2 seconds later watch fireworks (and I'm not actually exaggerating... most content can die in 1-2 firing salvos and there are some builds and weapons that hit unlimited targets for full damage in a firing cone in front of you, and there are abilities to help pull them all into a single group for your ease of doing this).  It takes longer vs bosses, but the concept is still the same.

3) To go with 2, there's no real separation of content for those just reaching max level and those that have been leveling up their gear for awhile and thus are really powerful in comparison.  The more powerful player can freely enter shared content with lower powered players, and then can run around and kill everything in seconds.  Often times the lower powered players don't even have time to reach the enemies to fire at them and thus are considered as having not contributed and will get no/reduced rewards, or even "afk" penalties.  While some content does have more advanced difficulty instances for these more powerful players, they're not obligated to use them, and not all content has these.

4) Lag.  For the past couple of years, they've been having increased issues with lag and "rubberbanding" (you essentially warp back to where you were a few moments ago), despite a decreased overall player count compared to when they opened.  At times it is atrocious.

So, again, while it is fun to play up through, there are other elements that can make it a bit frustrating, and there's nothing at the end to keep you wanting to play.  Once you reach a certain point, everything just dies when you look at it funny.  That gets old and boring really fast to me.

Fights start to drag on longer, with a whole lot more clicking, ability use, moving your ship, switching to shoot torpedoes or fighters, then remembering to click on the enemy again so you actually fire. More and more clicking.

I do like that they get to experiment with the story and universes, there are some of the series cast giving their voices to the game, and there are a few other mechanics to learn and invest time in.
These are not the core of the game though, eventually everything just circles back to combat, so play is mostly going to be based around it: Death by clicking.

As much as i love this game it has too many problems. mainly pay to win

Key thing to remember is "Free to Play" = "Pay to Win"

All the best ships and equipment are behind paywalls so you won't get any T6 ships without paying $$$ to open loot boxes or buying Zen credits.

That said, the game is ok but very dated. It certainly looks and feels like it was made in the early 2000's, gameplay is rather basic, NPC "AI" is primitive at best. The episode missions feature good stories, but some of the later missions just go on and on and on and get quite tiresome. Mission difficulty scales with player level which is good, until you hit the top levels (65) when the scaling seems to assume that you are using top tier ships and equipment (from loot boxes which cost $ to open). This means that they become very difficult if you aren't paying to win.

Some missions are bugged, usually involving scripted events not firing or unresponsive NPC's which can usually be got around by aborting the mission and retrying from the beginning. Very frustrating when you spend an hour getting to the final boss. Frequent issues with loadouts disappearing, traits resettings, bumping into invisible "forcefields", rubberbanding, and other lag based effects. Daily extended maintenance issues which seem to fail to address issues.

Away mission controls are horrendous out the box. I remapped the WASD keys to match every other game and using B to enter shooter mode makes it tolerable. Space combat I was imagining something like EVE Online, but instead its more like the old Star Trek Starfleet Command of the late 90's and hasn't been improved upon.

If you're really interested in Star Trek and want to explore the stories and lore then go ahead, if you're looking for a space based MMORPG or single player shooter experience then there are much better alternatives.

Oh, and there are no Steam achievements despite what the store page says.

I've played Star Trek Online since 2015 (Steam shows 100+ hours but I use the main launcher more, closer to 1000+ hours) and it is a good game but the game is plagued with issues. This is being written in 2023, so here is a 2023 point of view. 

TL;DR: The game is fun but end game is just grinding the same events over and over, while they shove another lootbox ship in your face that you probably won't be lucky enough to get and maybe the occasional new mission you'll finish in 30 minutes. 


First the good
- The gameplay itself is simplistic yet fun to play. It starts off a little slow but as you get closer to end game, you'll get access to more abilities and ships that really show the combat in STO. Ground combat is a little bland, but 90% of players will tell you the space combat makes STO what it is. It does have an addicting combat gameplay that does make you crave more. 
- Starship design is on point. The devs have really nailed making ship designs. Not all are great, but I'd say most are. 
- Although the game is pay to win, it's not difficult to play Free to Play. Though I've dropped money here and there myself, building a ship and ground equipment without spending a dime is actually fairly straight forward. Just do quests, dailies, missions, and TFOs you'll have Mk XV equipment in no time. Getting them to epic is harder, but over time can be achieved. Plus the STO community welcomes asking for help with building the perfect build, no matter the budget. 
- If you're a Star Trek fan you'll find something here you like story wise. The overall story is good, though later episodes have fallen in writing. More on that later. 
- Voice acting is actually really good, and getting Star Trek actors to play is just an amazing cherry on top. 

But now here are the issues
- The game is heavily favoring lootbox content over actual content releases these days. We haven't gotten a level cap or major update since Victory is Life (2018), the devs have stated most story/content updates are now just small. No more major content planned. This bummed me out, as they made getting to end game (currently level 65) much easier, but then are basically capping what end game is. The events they have are just completely repetitive. You do the same mission or TFO 10-21 times within whatever the timeframe to complete is. All to sometimes get things that aren't completely worth it. It gets boring to do this real quick, and then Cryptic dangles a "Well you can cut it short by paying us 2,000 Zen ($20 USD) to just finish it now". Content updates now consist of: 1 new mission, 1 new TFO (group mission), probably a lootbox ship or two and that's about it. Nothing to actually build your character more or, expand the STO galaxy they used to spend so much time expanding. UPDATE: Now the buy out is 2,500 Zen ($25, 25% increase) as if the $20 wasn't already too much for garbage. 

- The above leads to the power creep, and I don't necessarily mind a power creep, what I don't like is what to do with it. Yes we can crank the difficulty to Advanced or Elite, but after a while you work to beat those with ease too and once again you just kinda float staring at your space barbie. Speaking of...

- The big issue as stated in the first point is Cryptic has heavily favored lootbox content. Almost every month it's about a new lootbox ship that they want you to gamble on. And they HEAVILY favor Research and Development boxes now. Master keys are $1.25 USD a piece, but R&D boxes are $3 USD a pop. There are bundle deals but quite frankly, this is terrible. The drop rates are never shared so don't expect to find that. There is estimates online but Cryptic has never actually shared the true drop rate and by most people's calculations it definitely falls below a 1% chance. (0.1% chance is said quite often). They hype these up so much and when you ask them about something like new story content or major content updates, they just frown upon you during their stream of lootbox ship #247. When it's not a lootbox its a ship that's either $30, or a bundle locked behind a $100-$300 paywall, and don't even get me started on Mudd's market. 

- The writing in STO seems to have fallen a bit. What was once a game that told fantastic stories seems to not completely know what to do anymore. I feel they need to take a extended time writing the next chapter, just so they can really make something that is more compelling to be a part of. 

- Cryptic engine is definitely out of date. Game is buggy with many bugs never addressed and just brushed over. While I do put this down, they are not the only dev to do this in modern gaming and won't be the last either. The graphics are a bit dated, while I praise the starship design, and even some of the planet design is fantastic, it falls really short on facial animations. It almost compares to Skyrim in some cases. I am just waiting for one of them to fly in the air randomly to confirm this. 

This all leads to me finding it difficult to recommend this game... I wish steam had a middle ground recommend button like "use with caution" because when you first start you're probably going to love this game. However as you get to end game, you realize that's kind of it. If repetitive events and lootbox content with the occasional semi-poorly written mission is your thing, go for it. But if you're looking for a Star Trek adventure that really explores the final frontier, it's almost dead in the water here. I hope the devs make more content that actually involves updating the content but until then, I worry you may be disappointed once you reach the end.

This game is charming at first. It can be fun and will be fun for the beginning. In all honesty, you will probably have a blast at first. The space combat feels good and is probably one of the best points in the game. The ground combat is a little janky, but it does the job mostly well and I have never had any issues with it. So why do I not recommend this? Well, the game does what a lot of MMO's do and makes the mid-late game near impossible unless you pay money. Now it does take a while to get there, but you will know once you do. It becomes impossible to get new ships (the currency required to get ships beyond a certain point is pay only) it becomes impossible to get new and better weapons (again pay only), and the difficulty of the missions do not decrease to compensate. You can get pretty far, but you will reach the point where you really can't progress any further and you'll know it. 

On top of that, while this is a good MMO game (at least for the early-mid parts) it is NOT a good STAR TREK game. this game involves a lot of combat, gunning, fighting, etc. with most "science" or "engineering" solutions involving hitting the action button in a specific spot. Only on rare occasions does talking actually get you anywhere, you pretty much never have fun random encounters (everything occurs on missions), and, while you can technically explore your ship, it is really empty and not actually there (funnily enough this is where the console version is better because on PC ship interiors are locked behind a pay wall and only the main command spot is open, but on console all the ship interiors are free and you can explore the whole ship without issues as well). There are only a few missions that take place inside your ship, and they don't care what interior you are set to have.

Overall, give the game a try, it is free, but once you hit that pay-wall point, just stop. The game does not improve and it only has a few "that is clever" game design moments. You are probably better off trying out bridge crew or playing EVE/Elite and Dangerous.

Where to begin with this game.....Well, for starters, it doesn't seem to know what KIND of game it is. It's a Space Sim, no wait, it's a Space Tactics game, no wait, it's a 3PS with literally the worst controls and gameplay I've ever experienced, (and I lived through the MS-DOS era of gaming), no, now it wants to be an MMO! I get that Star Trek encompasses all of these genres, but this game seems to think that being terrible at most of them is better than being good at one of them.

Next, we get into the real hot-topic of this game being P2W. Without exception, it's 100% pay to win. The wait times for prizes are excessive, and you HAVE to buy keys to unlock these "prize boxes". So yes, it's pay to win or put more accurately: if you don't pay, you're going to respawn insanely often.

Let's also consider that the game has been in development for 15 years now. 15 years! And they still haven't figured out how to make ground combat manageable without having to click on (up to) 100 individual tiles. The graphics still meet the bare minimum definition of the word "graphics" as we knew it in 2015, and in 2025, there's just no excuse for loading issues and horrendous hit boxes anymore. I can't even get into the stupendously clunky control schemes without going into a full on rant about keyboard efficiency and effective gameplay.

Overall, I give this game a 3/10. It tried hard to give us the entire Star Trek experience, but only resulted in a 
pretty awful all around experience wrapped in a Pay 2 Win package that used fans' love of Star Trek to make absurd amounts of money. I feel bad for the OG Trek actors who provided their voices to this game, for being associated with a total scam. I also feel bad for Terry Matalas for giving this game a shout out (via the Enterprise F's cameo) in Picard Season 3. That was a huge shout out, Cryptic, the Enterprise F has been etched into Star Trek Canon now, and it comes back to this complete scam of a game. The fact that we have to live with the STO Enterprise F forever in Star Trek lore now is probably the thing that disgusts me the most about this game. The best season of Picard, the TNG comeback we've wanted for 20+ years, and it's sullied by Star Trek Online.

"The pricing is truly truly truly outrageous. Oh ho ho yeah. $30 for ONE ship. $5.50 for a costume. $12.50 to make your ship's bridge look like the Enterprise-D. Everything is just a little more expensive than you would expect.

Tier 6 ships (the highest tier, I believe) cost 3000 zen. 3000 zen costs $30. You can earn dilithium ore in-game by completing daily missions and repeating "Task Force Operations". (Which are equivalent to dungeons in most mmos.) You can refine up to 8000 dilithium ore per day. The refined version can be exchanged for zen. However, the exchange rate is roughly 500 dilithium for 1 zen.

So to obtain a $30 ship for "free", you would need nearly 1.5 million units of refined ore. At a rate of 8k per day, this requires around 180 days.

Assuming you login and gain the 8k every single day. Which is estimated to take a little under 4 hours. That's 720 hours of your life you are never getting back. For a $30 ship. That's like working for $0.04 per hour. No way I'm doing that! That's not even remotely reasonable." -Jackie Daytona

This is a bad game unfortunate to wear the Star Trek name.

Sure it starts off quite fun with a lot of veneer on the surface as you start to recognise the voiced actors from the various shows. But after getting blown up for the umpteenth time in ship-to-ship combat, I wish I could get my money back!

What's that? It's a free-to-play game, you say?

I know, but I still feel like I've been cheated.

The game is woeful in its tutorial only teaching you the basics whilst expecting you to trawl through menu upon menu to find extra keybinds you didn't know your character could benefit from that WOULD HAVE BEEN NICE TO KNOW AT THE TUTORIAL LEVEL!

I can't stand games like this; they look like they're promising you so much, until you sink some time into them and you quickly realise that an awful lot of boot polish has been applied onto a wooden statue only to be clobbered over the head by said statue.

The space combat is so lacklustre that you find yourself dying over and over again without ever really knowing what you're doing wrong. You just get spanked (and not in a good way!). Hints would be welcome if you keep dying to the same foes (who magically regenerate all their health when you go right back in by the way!) to at least offer you some guidance what you need to upgrade.

I haven't got time to source external sites for data to study which weapon combinations are better than others for my ships when I game TO RELAX not for endless frustration at doing different things over and over again but getting the same RNG results. It's utter cr@p!

I wanted to like this, I really did, but I just can't recommend it for what I've got out of it... hair-tearing frustration at seeing your ship get destroyed because the RNG loot drops you get after a fight just WON'T give you the weapons that give you a fighting change against enemies you should be obliterating.

This is looter-shooter at it's most banal and I haven't got anymore time to waste without having something more substantial to show for it.

If you ignore this review, then that's your call, just know I don't want you to have anywhere near the frustration I've had when other games are actually ENJOYABLE to play!

Pros : 
          - It's star trek!
          - There's actually kind of a story. Some of it not bad at all.
          - they made a pretty decent effort with their character creation elements.
          - you kinda get to make a whole party, and can customise their appearances, so yes, you can have a pretty female bridge crew wearing skirts


Cons:
          - terrible, dated graphics that kinda feel like PS2/PS3 era.
          - Story & immersion is undone by MMORPG elements, i.e.: no failure states, respawning, reliance on gear etc.
         - Immersion is ruined by the faction system butting up against what should be the plot, this is best explained with examples, for instance, Romulans and Jem'Hadar must join starfleet or the klingon empire, which can now use ships from these races. The klingon missions are often about honour and klingon society and such, but your character may not be a klingon. Also, federation content is reused for much of the klingon stuff.
        - Whilst you can technically get premium currency for free, you can get roughly 22 premium currency a day as you are limited to the amount of dilithium you can refine. The things you want cost 3,000 premium currency. It's designed to make you want to spend real world money.
       - It feels very strange for star trek models to be shooting at one another, chewing through masses of shields and hit points or hull integrity, this is very unlike the franchise.
      - a lot of the game can be played solo, so the game doesn't seem very social to me, I'm only 70+ hours in, but haven't spoken to another player yet.
     - this raises the crux of my problem with this game, it would have been a much, much better experience if it was made as a single player game, the content trimmed down into higher quality stuff, rather than needing to produce the mounds of chaff that MMORPGs need, and so on, but, well, MMORPGs must be more profitable.
      - the endgame is gruellingly hard, and requires ruthless management of equipment, with only specific playstyles and loadouts and such being playable. In fact, many missions are best done when you are low level, as the enemies if anything over-scale as you level up. Yeah, the endgame really saps the joy out of it for me, and makes me want to stop playing with my max level characters.
      - absolutely chock full of bugs, I encounter one every 2-5 hours. Most of the time you can fix them by dropping the quest and then re-acquiring it, but it's still a pain in the ass. (and this game is 10 years old!)
     - you have to wait for background tasks to complete, just like Neverwinter.
-they're stopping support for windows 7 soon, won't be able to play any more soon, I can go to hell it would seem.

Overall, play only if you're a megafan like myself, and don't expect this game to leave a huge impression on you.

Edit : yeah, the endgame is just too punishingly difficult, try a mission at levels 45 - 55 and then the same thing at 65 and the 65 mission is just too difficult. It seems to me to be a way to encourage you to buy premium currency, but I'm uninstalling instead. Games shouldn't become un-playable in difficulty as you increase in level.

I say this but there are some major issues so that I feel forced to not recommend this to other players:

a) the game hides information from you - maybe that is strongly worded but it certainly feels like it when you pick a race and find out later: they have stats or rather abilities attached to them! But you are in for 20 levels now, want to restart because you dislike your starting race boni?

b) the game is unable to communicate clearly what you need to know - it is in fact so obscure that one guide for this game will fail dramatically to convey important information. You might even read multiple guides and still have a limited and fractured understanding of what is going on. God knows I am past level 40 and the amount of things I don't know yet is extreme.

c) bugs - there is tons of them - ranging from minor to major.
Minor such as your quest indicator doesn't count when you do parts of a mission and never turns green indicating that this part of the mission is done.
Major: I kept flying while I scanned a mission objective - the mission objective disabled my ship and the mission assumed I would be close enough to beam aboard said objective - I wasn't, so I was stuck on a disabled ship unable to do anything. I figured out a work around but stuff like this is way too common for a ten year old game which brings me to:

d) zero polish - dare I say that the HUD is atrocious? The design is userunfriendly and looks ancient.
After years you can find old reddit discussions adressing the bugs mentioned above.
The Federation tutorial is too long, corny and destroys immersion.

e) minor gripes - I have an endless list but one of many is - you meet the same enemy ships they just are higher level. Combat also makes no sense in terms of actual power levels of the ships you fly in Universe:
You meet and kill in one mission a vor'cha and two d7s with your Miranda class. *sigh* You kill a D'Deridex Warbird in a T'Liss .... hello?
There are these missions where you can say to yourself: I guess I just sit here and wave from the bridge of my Sovereign class while enemy b just tractors enemy a's ship away - these are extremely frustrating cut scenes.

F) gound combat - its bad

Anyway, on a positive note: its free and your choice to torment yourself with the stuff I mentioned above. I certainly keep doing so, god knows why.
Also I suppose that the company spends most of the time on new end game content, so if you get there and you have fun playing with friends, I don't think any of the stuff mentioned above matters much.

But for new players? Not recommended.

Star Trek Online (STO) is worth a try. [i]If[/i] you're a Trekkie. Otherwise, it's just outdated graphics and stale gameplay. It's entertaining, but quickly becomes repetitive.

There's a lot I could say about the game. Instead, I'd like to focus on the one aspect that led me to leave a negative review: the monetization.

The game is f2p. So, I expected microtransactions, and such. I was totally unprepared. Their in-game store contains [i]thousands[/i] of dollars of merchandise. This is not a game in which you are going to own everything. (Unless you are crazy-rich.)

The pricing is truly truly truly outrageous. Oh ho ho yeah. $30 for ONE ship. $5.50 for a costume. $12.50 to make your ship's bridge look like the Enterprise-D. Everything is just a little more expensive than you would expect.

Fans on the forums will tell you, "Yeah, but you can just grind and buy the stuff for free." This is true. You absolutely [i]can[/i] work to get the items for free. However, the time investment is hardly worth it.

The system is complicated. Try to follow me. 

Tier 6 ships (the highest tier, I believe) cost 3000 zen. 3000 zen costs $30. You can earn dilithium ore in-game by completing daily missions and repeating "Task Force Operations". (Which are equivalent to dungeons in most mmos.) You can refine up to 8000 dilithium ore per day. The refined version can be exchanged for zen. However, the exchange rate is roughly 500 dilithium for 1 zen.

So to obtain a $30 ship for "free", you would need nearly 1.5 million units of refined ore. At a rate of 8k per day, this requires around 180 days. 

Assuming you login and gain the 8k every single day. Which is estimated to take a little under 4 hours. That's 720 hours of your life you are never getting back. For a $30 ship. That's like working for $0.04 per hour. No way [i]I'm[/i] doing that! That's not even remotely reasonable.

(Edit: [b]To be fair,[/b] there's an easier way to obtain a free T6 ship. It's simply a matter of waiting for one of several yearly events. Then completing dailies until you get the required number of points.)

Oh, and loot boxes. With variable rarities. In other words, gambling. Because spending $3 on a box, $1.25 on a key to open it, and then getting a mundane item you could have acquired anywhere isn't at all exploitative.

STO isn't against twisting your arm. They hook me up with 4 bridge officers. Then 2 more, but they won't let me use the new ones. Why? Because I don't have enough "bridge officer slots". The only way to obtain more is to delete one I already have. OR spend money to unlock the slots.

Why even bother? Because my ship has 7 positions for bridge officers. Not being able to fill all the positions puts me at a disadvantage. In particular, my science station is empty. Due to this, I am denied an extra ability in space combat.

So, I need to buy 3 slots. However, the game only sells slots 2 at a time for $3 each. But the game will only sell me zen in amounts of $5 or $10. Which means I need $6 worth of zen for my ship to be fully-functional. So, I'm forced to buy $10, and then have 400 zen left I don't intend to use. Worse, I'm pretty sure you have to spend this with every character you make. (If you want to fill those positions.)

I really wanted to talk about the gameplay. Particularly, the space combat. However, none of it is worth it.

This game wants your money, and everything is centered around getting you to spend. I can't support a game like that. At least, not financially.

I will, however, still play for free. I'd like to see if the game has any more to offer that might change my mind.

Update: Playing more [i]did[/i] change my mind. Started to really enjoy it. Learned about more f2p options. Gonna go ahead and leave this a negative review. A game with graphics this dated (running on Dx9, no less.) has no reason to do this. No flaws of Win7 are a threat to STO in any way.

Despite a few nice fan moments – like flying a Galaxy-class ship or meeting familiar characters – the aftertaste is bitter.

I pre-ordered the Collector's Edition. While I'm not the biggest Star Trek fan, I agree with others that STO may be the best Trek game out there - unfortunately, that says more about the state of Trek gaming than anything. I haven't played much since 2012, but I pop my head in every few years because the space combat is addicting. 

I would prefer not to downvote this game, but unfortunately, it has some significant issues that cannot be overlooked:

[list]
    [*]It is a 15-year old MMORPG. Like all older MMOs, the newer content looks good with better animations and higher resolution textures. But, when bumped up against older content and models, they stand out. This is universal with all MMOs. 
    [*]Ground combat sucks. It sucked in 2010 and especially in 2025. Cryptic attempted to "modernize" it over the years, but it's not great. Space combat is amazing - even non-Trek fans should enjoy it. 
    [*]STO's monetization strategy makes mobile games blush. End game ships run $25-30 each. Bundles of ships with additional perks are $100+. Many players justify these costs - if you're devoting dozens or hundreds of hours a year, it may balance out. To the more casual fan, it does not. [b]Remember:[/b] There is no subscription for STO. It's F2P or Zen store. 
[/list]

[h3] My Recommendation [/h3]
Try it out. Level up some characters. There are some free T6 (end game) ships available through events - although they're a slugfest to get and likely not the "cool ones," that you may want. Since it is F2P, it doesn't hurt to try.

I've been watching Star Trek since I was a wee lad. I started with the ST:OS, ST:tNG is my favorite series followed by The Orville, Enterprise then Voyager. I give you the above to give you a little insight into what I like about the universe. To me ST is about exploration, discovery, science and technology, working together as a crew to over come challenges and using violence as a last resort. The Federation is about unity, equality and mutual benefit. Star Fleet is there to push and defend those ideas. Politics and intrigue was always part of the sphere as well and became more prominent in some series than others. DS9 was more about politics than any before or after.  

Star Trek is not about ship to ship battles and away team CQB. Yet that is what most of my experience with the game has been. Sadly formulaic. Get a mission, arrive at the location, enter a ship battle, finish ship battle, beam to the location, enter CQB, end CQB, beam back to ship and enter a ship to ship battle. I really wanted to like this game. It has a lot of great ideas, and it uses a more naval-feeling format of space combat than the standard dog-fight-ey fare, and of course- Star Trek. Lots of fun to be had with that franchise.

The problem is that it's built on the same engine as Neverwinter, and suffers from lots of the same issues. Foremost, the system of warcraft-esque trays upon trays of abilities and cooldowns seems both tired and uncharacteristic for what the game is supposed to represent. During space combat, you're expected to do the job of every bridge officer at once, and the result is that you simply can't do any of them well. Even if you devoted all of your attention to one aspect of flying the ship, you still couldn't do it as well as you should be able to because the controls have been simplified so that you can do all the other stuff too. Tbh, this just seems lazy in a game that exists at the same time as Artemis. 

Space combat isn't even the reason I'm quitting though- the real issue is that the moment you're on the ground, you're stuck playing something that should CLEARLY be an FPS, but isn't. There is no option not to autotarget your shots, the autotargeting system is terrible, and movement maneuvers like dodging are treated like skills so they queue behind any other skills you've hit the buttons for rather than interrupting, meaning not only do you stand in front of a slow moving shot like a moron, but then you dive in a random direction afterwards for no apparent reason. Usually at that point you get your ass handed to you by idiot AIs who wouldn't have gotten anywhere near you if the game were a real FPS like Destiny or something.

I really really wish I liked this game; the only thing I wish more is that I hadn't wasted so much time trying to convince myself it was worth playing when it REALLY isn't. Too bad though; I wonder if they'll ever make a Star Trek game worth playing...

I have been playing this game fairly consistently for the past 8 or so years. I also lead an in-game Fleet (Guild) that has had a constant player base that has grown and shrunk over time with sometimes hundreds of people. In other words, I truly love this game and almost always have enjoyed playing it.

Which makes what I'm about to say very hard.

Over these years the game has steadily become one of the most greediest, dirtiest cash grabs in the current Free-to-Play MMO market. It takes literal months to grind (and I mean GRIND) for a free, premium ship. Even other free ships, like the summer/winter event ones, still require weeks of grinding - and it NEVER changes. They don't change these events, so every year it's the same activities. which becomes extremely dull extremely fast. 

Not to mention EVERYTHING else in the game requires a purchase. Uniforms, lockbox keys, bridge officers, playable factions, inventory slots, bank slots, ship slots, duty officers, shuttles, equipment upgrades, etc. While some fans may attack me and say that not ALL of these items are only attainable through real money purchases, it is MUCH easier to buy them than to grind for them.

Another in-game currency, Dilithium, has had a very small cap that has never changed for countless years. This currency allows you to upgrade your gear, support your Fleet, buy special equipment you unlock through Reputations (which, of course, require a little bit of grinding, but not nearly as bad as the previously mentioned gripes) and other useful items. The cap is insultingly low, and once again, some fans may say "well, you can refine a little extra from your Fleet mine!" or "If you're a lifetime member, you can refine an extra 1,000 every few days". Of course, lifetime subscriptions cost $200-$300, assuming they're on sale. Obviously a small price to pay for a little extra dilithium that can only be initiated through a certain mission on a certain planet.

This is only scratching the surface of this game's issues. A lot of the older missions have loads of bugs and are simply outdated (think Nimbus), some of the newer ones have some too, the engine has been out of date for years and they show no sign of upgrading it, and there's just so many bugs sometimes. I can recall when expansions would drop and certain missions or activities would literally cause your game to crash. I understand some of these times bugs will happen, but Cryptic never seems to truly test their new content. 

I am truly saddened and sickened by how awful the monetisation methods have become in this game. Like I said, I still do love this game, but I don't recommend new players to try it right now. I PRAY that they will eventually realize the insanity behind their practices and actually put some love and effort into this game, but until they do, you're better off playing older Star Trek games like Armada.

The truth is far worse: if you say something - even in obvious jest - they will ban you from the game.

They also - FOR SOME REASON - don't include anti-semitism.

Now, I know some people that haven't fallen into those stated categories, but got banned anyway purely because A GM TOOK OFFENCE.

Said people tried raising this issue up with other GM's, clearly pointing out to them that the GM in question overstepped their authority and banned them for typing something they didn't like.
No, it wasn't racist, sexist, spamming, gold sales, or anything else.

-> The GM just didn't like it. <-

Strange right, that the game based on Gene Roddenberry's creation where everybody should have a voice and get along doesn't live up to it's creator's wish, because the GM's won't let you speak freely.

I know someone that mocked the current socio-political situation in America, even putting what they said in speech marks, typing out what someone of low intelligence would say. 

A GM banned them for "political campaigning".
F***ING SERIOUSLY?! Banned for an obvious joke?!

Now, in the EULA there's NOTHING in there that says you're not allowed to do "political campaigning" (which they weren't, they were mocking it), but despite trying to argue with a different GM, they closed ranks and refused to undo what they've done, even though their actions were clearly wrong.

Thing is, THEY DON'T EVEN LIVE IN AMERICA - they're in the U.K.

They like to say you have "Freedom of Speech" in their game, but they're lying - they will ban you for minor things just because a GM doesn't like it and NOTHING YOU SAY WILL CHANGE THIS.

I've seen some horrendous comments in this game's zone chat. Racism, sexism, you name it - I've seen it all happen with GM's present without them batting an eyelid.
But make a joke they don't like and they censor you with a ban. 
Make a statement they don't like and they censor you with a ban.

The ban will lock you out initially for 24hrs, but after 3 of them, they outright ban you permanently.

The sad part is (even without the violation of your right to speak freely and openly), this game simply isn't worth it.


Now on to the game itself:

-> THIS GAME HAS HAD PRACTICALLY NO NEW CONTENT FOR OVER TEN YEARS. <-

Let that sink in for a sec.

TEN YEARS, and their "new content" - for an MMO mind you - is one (two if you're lucky) "episodes", or missions if you will, that lasts for about an hour of game-play. 

Oh and a metric f*** ton of "lock box" ships with impossible odds, but lets face it, that's not actually CONTENT is it?

It's possible to grind a max level character out in 3 days. Again, this is an MMO - hitting max level should take way longer. No, I'm not talking about spending three whole days with no sleep and a bunch of snack food and energy drinks around you while you do it. 
I'm talking three days of a few hours of playtime per day.

I know because I've done it.

They like to make a big deal about how you can play one of four factions. The reality is that one faction is only playable once you have a max level character. Once unlocked, you get to pick a jem'hadar at max level. 
Woo.
All the levelling's been done for you.
Cor. 
So the other three factions?
Klingon, Federation, Romulan. Except that at level 10, as a Romulan you have to "pick" if you're allied with the klingons or federation. 

This means your technically down to 2 factions. 

But wait - this isn't over yet: past the first half dozen or so klingon missions, you aren't doing their missions anymore. You're doing FEDERATION missions. Because the dev's are too lazy to create new content for these other factions.

Want to be an awesome klingon warrior captaining a bird of prey? That'll feel awesome for about 10 minutes, then you're wondering why you're doing stuff for some federation clown.

Want to be a sneaky romulan, invading federation space and stealing their secrets and engaging in industrial sabotage and spying? Yeah, that doesn't happen - you end up being some weird civilian refugee that has to pick a side. 

Great - so on point.

End game content?
Basically just running the same group missions over and over for faction points so you can trade them for faction gear. 
You might ask about PVP but in reality that's pretty unbalanced thanks to all the game's "premium content", so very few actually play it (I seem to remember that at some point, one of the higher-ups in the dev food chain was openly against PVP, and tried to kill it off outright) and if you do, it usually ends up being very one-sided, and certainly isn't fun.

The tech running the game is ancient. It was old almost twenty years ago when the game was new.
The graphics are sub par.
Is your character voice acted? Nope. You might as well call your character "Captain Mime" - they gesticulate when someone talks to them, but sure as heck don't verbalise back.

The voice acting is practically non-existent outside of specifically voiced segments.
Because of these segments, (which the game's dev's will gush about how they managed to get these out of work, low paid sci-fi actors to do a little VA work to their scripts,) they expect you to sink cash into the game for their minimal expenditure at trying to make a game of this nature competitive with other MMO's on the market, all the while trying to fish for those 'member berries for the TV series and films. 
I mean, for crying out loud, Age of Conan is older and it has better VA work.

So how do they sting you for all your cash? The usual:

Lock boxes. Account unlocks. Cosmetics. Premium Currencies.
Are you gonna charge me when I get up and take a pee too?!

This game is a greedy, predatory cash grab claiming to be free, but at the end of the game (I.E. where you're max level) they stop giving you "free" ships, so you have to scrape by or open the wallet just so you don't do a regular one player mission and get utterly schooled by trash mobs.

The loot boxes are as you'd expect: great rewards at ridiculous odds:
1. Buy a key for a couple of bucks.
2. Open box.
3. Fail to get anything of value.
4. Repeat. 
That's the trap they want you in, while they greedily go on about how "great" the top prizes are, without openly telling you that your chance of getting the top prize is about 0.5% PER BOX.

Okay, I originally gave this game a thumbs up, but I've changed my mind.

There are some massive problems.

False Controller Fully Supported Claim.
1. The information here on Steam says that it is fully controller compatible. This isn't true. There are many key commands on a keyboard that you simply cannot do with your controller.

2. If you're expecting to log on for the first time, build your character and be able to use your controller to its full capabilities, you'll be angrily disappointed. The reality is, in order to get the most out of your controller you'll have to learn to write a programming file to assign your keybinds to which controller buttons, or combination of buttons you want. Oh, and just so that you know: the information on how to do that on the "official" wiki is NOT correct. Even many other independent sites don't have all the info you'll need to get it done correctly. And trying to find a full list of keybinds somewhere on the internet will have you pulling your hair out (if you have any).

The Official Wiki Nonsense:
There really isn't much helpful information about how to perform certain actions on the wiki, for instance, if you don't know how to "commission a bridge officer", if you go to the wiki for help of how to do that, all it says is to "commission the bridge officer" but absolutely no steps all about what to actually do to make that happen. And the reality is, there aren't any wikis or help sites at all that give you any explanations about how to do anything in this game at all.

Inherent Programming Problems
There are a LOT of these and Cryptic has shown no interest in fixing them. In one Episode/Mission/Quest called "Colliseum" there's a worm type creature sticking out of the ground you need to defeat to continue. On THREE different characters I wasn't able to hurt it, and it wasn't hurting me. Yet, I couldn't beam out of the arena to try and restart. I tried to drop the mission and do something else, but no, that didn't work either. I had to stand there with my character for nearly an hour before the programming decided to fix itself. And this was on each character. And no, exiting the game, restarting Steam and everything didn't fix the problem either.

2. Completely useless allies. There are lots of times on ground and in space where you are surrounded with allies that are supposed to help you in the fight. However, most of them won't do anything at all. And if you're not sure how to max out your ship or ground gear, you can literally be trying to defeat an enemy ship or boss for over an hour and not getting anywhere because your allies aren't doing anything. I had one ally that I called in with my captain abilities as backup, and that ship went to the other side of the map to attack something that wasn't part of my mission objective at the time. And there was nothing I could do. There is a keybind that is supposed to make your allies attack your target and help you out, but shocker, it didn't work. Again, Cryptic hasn't done anything about this.

3. User Interface (UI) failures: When you have a certain ability assigned to particular button, your skill bar will show that it is ready to be used, but when you press that button, the slotted ability will light up, but it won't activate. You need to try again with no guarantee it'll work that time either. Once again, the developers don't care at all.

4. Unneed and repeating cutscenes.
There are just way too many cutscenes in this game, and I would argue only a few of them are actually needed. What's worse, some of these overly long cutscenes will play twice and not once. And of course, if you have issues with an episode/mission not working properly, the help desk will tell you that if you've skipped cutscenes by holding down the ESC key, then guess what, it'll cause programming issues. So, if you want to avoid a chance your game messing up, you'll have to watch the same long cutscences twice in a row.

5. Overuse of Borg.
Just like with Marvel and the current "superhero fatigue" there's been quite a bit of Borg fatigue in the Star Trek fandom for quite awhile. Ever since the series Voyager overdid the Borg nonsense fans have been pretty sick of it, and this game just makes it even worse. Not only do you need to deal with your universe's Borg, but the Mirror Universe Borg (which in one quest like Mirror Janeway is the Borg Queen, and in the next quest line, Janeway hasn't died, but now Harry Kim is the "Borg King" apparently the developers can't remember what they've done from one quest line to the other), then you need to deal with yet another universe's "Control Borg". Oh, and it doesn't end there ... there's aliens that basically very tall "little green men" ... they turn out to be Borg too from yet ANOTHER universe. If that's not bad enough, semi-"normal" Borg tend to show up and attack you in space in missions that really have NOTHING to do with them. Over half of this game, I'd say even around 3/4 of this game is dealing with Borg, and that's about it. Better get used to it. Even though there's many other foes in the Star Trek Universe they could write stories about, nope, you're getting Borg. There's only one mission out of all of them that deal with the Kazon, but the Borg, you'll get to the point that you're going to get so bored of it that you tend to roll your eyes like "oh boy ... more Borg ... big shocker there ..." note the sarcasm.

5. Supernatural nonsense.
I don't know if current gamers are familiar with the old tabletop RPG "RIfts" basically sci-fi mixed with magic and fighting demons, but in the Klingon quest line and in the "Klingon Civil War" (available to all factions) you're not only going into Klingon "Hell" but also having these demons show up in the real world (in the Klingon quest line) and also "demon ships" (in both quest lines). It's like the developers just ripped of Rifts, and in a very lame and uninteresting way. Star Trek has always been about "hard sci-fi", this isn't a sci-fantasy franchise, please keep it that way.

The 2025 Delta Event.
This one is real surprise. In the event page in game, it says that you need to complete Episodes to get the rewards, however, the reality is that you need to complete Accolades/Achievements to get them. Anyone who plays MMO's can tell you that Missions/Quests and Achievements are NOT the same thing. Yet, the support people will keep trying to justify it with a "work around". The problem is, they knew this information wasn't true before the event went live, I know this from their own statements.

So, here's a definition from legeldictionary.net:
"As a legal term, false advertising refers to any published claim or advertising material that gives consumers an incorrect understanding or belief about a product or service being offered."

The incorrect information given in the game itself for this event fits that definition. The service or "event" that was offered rewards under conditions "x" was knowingly incorrect and led to who knows who many people wondering why they weren't receiving the rewards.

Has Arc offered to fix the problem and compensate the customers who spent days to gain these rewards? No. Because we're supposed to complete the Achievements, and not the Episodes like the Event in game says to.

I spent a good deal of time trying to get Cryptic to fix their mistake, but they simply wouldn't.

It's been out for 10 years and it's STILL a damned buggy mess. I want to like this game because I love all Trek (except JJTrek because I'm not a [i]sociopath[/i]), but I just cannot enjoy STO with the constant rubberbanding and server timeouts. FPS drops and visual bugs are still persistent since launch, and will apparently never be fixed. Then again, why fix the game's engine or servers, when you can just sell three hundred dollar ship bundles to the whales you've addicted through applied gambling mechanics (as advised by your paid "gaming psychologists")? This game sucks, and Perfect World Entertainment is an undisputed cancer on the modern online gaming landscape.

EDIT: Came back for the "Year of Klingon," only to find the game still sucks considerably. The engine is still trash, the servers still completely unstable. Lootboxes/MTX (and the pay-to-win issues it creates) have only gotten more aggressive. They've actually [i]removed[/i] a considerable amount of content and shuffled the remaining pieces around, claiming it's "a new experience." Yes, [i]technically[/i], it is. None of the early content is [i]bug-free[/i], and what they've done to it isn't [i]any good[/i], but it sure is "a new [way to] experience [old content]."

The new content, by the way, just isn't very good. The writing is both uninspired and unsurprising. Cutscenes and dialogue are a bugged-up [i]mess[/i]. My character didn't animate at all during several cutscenes (at one point straight-up T-posing, to my hilarious dismay). Many missions would play dialogue over top of other dialogue, all during combat, resulting in an incomprehensible jumble of every NPC yelling all at once. Sadly, the so-called "action gameplay" is still just a lazy DPS race where you tab target and mash keys to make big numbers. Missions are decidedly boring, and feel too similar in scope and design:
1) Talk to NPCs
2) Shoot enemies
3) Warp to new sector
4) Pew pew pew
5) [i]Pew pew pew[/i]
6) Warp [i]again[/i]
7) Maybe pew pew pew
8) Watch completely broken cutscene
9) Get 3-10+ utterly forgettable technobabble-named rewards you'll replace in another mission or two
10) Repeat

It's not a good look. The game loop in STO is bland, and has been since launch. Ship combat is only marginally better than ground combat, but both suffer from the same equally terrible (and archaic) game design--seriously, who in the hell actually [i]wants[/i] to mash four hotbars with 12 skills each in 2023? Not me. Thanks to this bad design, DPS is literally the [i]only[/i] thing that matters; melt enemy ship, win game. Leveling up your officers and selecting their skills outright [i]sucks[/i] and feels completely unrewarding; you're converting new officers into training manuals nine times out of ten. I should be [i]excited[/i] for my new Orion tactical officer candidate, not debating turning them into a damn book to give my disruptors like +5 DPS every 30 seconds.

STO's writing... god, it sucks. Trek has always had its corny moments, but this isn't even that. It's all so dour and bland, no heart to be found. War, war, war--all the time, space war. Even the fantastic DS9, [i]which was mostly about war[/i], knew how to laugh when things got too tense. What's worse, though, is that no actor carries any expansion well enough for me to care about any of its characters or events. PWE/Cryptic's handful of in-house actors are terrible, but since they're cheaper than any of the Trek regulars, you'll hear these in-housers [i]all the time[/i]; the same three voices, every single mission, doing nothing to sound any better than their performances from 10+ years ago. Lines are all obviously recorded separately; [i]no one[/i] is playing off the energy/performance of other actors, and it really shows when almost nobody can bring that sort of energy on their own. There [i]are[/i] veteran Trek actors to be found here (like Tim Russ and Kate Mulgrew, who kick ass and know their characters), but the voice [i]direction[/i] for these actors is clearly terrible. It's frustrating because Trek has proven time and again it can be [i]way[/i] better than... whatever the hell all this is.

As a final note, there are ship bundles costing [i][b]TWO HUNDRED AND FIFTY AMERICAN DOLLARS[/b][/i], on top of the game [i]still[/i] having expensive lockbox gambling. Predatory as all hell, an unsurprising par for the course with Perfect World Entertainment, and immensely sad to see shoehorned into a beloved franchise like Star Trek. Only a Ferengi would approve of such greedy bullshit.

Do not play this game, [i]especially[/i] if you love Star Trek.

Like all Trek properties, they now must conform with CBS guidelines and canon. This means a lot of content (foundry missions especially, which was a great way to engage the fan base) has been removed. Some would say those missions were bad, but there were some good ones in the mix. Removing the Guardian at the Edge of Forever was a crime and a loss to all fans of Star Trek. Remixing everything just so it can comply with and incorporate the new Trek stuff is abysmal as well. I thought the writing on the show was garbage till I played some of the new content. Your personal stance on that may vary, but dialog wise and story wise, the new stuff is terrible and lacks the charm of all the older series in my humble opinion.

Voice talent gets shuffled around based on who is persona non grata. Old voice actors will have lines dubbed over in favor of new ones that are done by actors who don't engage in wrong-think. What is wrong think? Whatever CBS says it is. As for the most obvious one of Vic Mignogna who voiced Admiral Garret, if you looked into that situation at all, you would know it was bullshit. Yes, he lost a case in court, but defamation suits are VERY hard to win, and require evidence that is so overwhelmingly damning, you could very well never see one won in your lifetime (outside of Johnny Depp who HAD said evidence). 

Echeb used to be at K-7. Now, because the real life actor that played Echeb has been blacklisted by CBS (wither he was in the wrong or not is irrelevant to this) and killed off in Picard as a sick writers way of getting their copium in, that character has been removed from game. In the beginning of this games life, it was explained that much of what would take place is in a parallel timeline. Why? Because Paramount was doing the new films and wanted that to be the brand going forward. Since that was the case, they had no reason to remove the character outside of it clashed with CBS's new canon storyline.

A very real issue, outside of the CBS entanglements, is the microtransaction hell this game was created on. It got worse as it changed hands and is now in the hands of Gearbox, who just suck the life out of games they had no hand in making. I expect if not for the EU punishing game companies for lootbox crap, this game would never have a campaign to earn premium stuff. This is a garbage giveaway anyways because it does not account unlock AND it takes an entire year to finish across multiple events. Miss one event, you can still grind to the end. Miss two and you are s**t outta luck. 

Another issue that is game specific is the player exchanges (both dilithium and energy credits). 

With respect to the dilithium exchange, it has been beyond broken for years now. The developers implemented ways to earn huge amounts of dilithium in game, but failed to implement any sort of limits to the exchanges to prevent it from inflating. Time to learn folks: Inflation is caused by one thing, and one thing only. Introduction more of something into a market. If that introduction is rapid and high volume, it causes massive inflation. 

While the developers keep saying they are trying to fix this, the only solution outside of changing currency types (again, as they did this before) would be to cut off, 100%, all dilithium sources until such time as the playerbase had expended their stockpiles thru various in game purchases. This also means making things available in the dilithium store that people want to buy, which there is precious little in there at the moment.

With respect to the energy credits exchange, this genuinly got addressed ONCE, and only once. The devs found many players selling things for more than the exchange would allow for a price limit, so they upped the limit. This in turn led to the players to continue selling things to each other directly for more than the exchange would allow, just now at a higher price.

 I have space bucks (energy credits) to spend because I knew how to get currency in game, but this is a huge wall for new players and they will hit it hard. Outside of spending cash for zen, buying stuff off the zen store and then selling it for energy credits, most new players will never even hit 1 billion credits (queue Dr Evil montage). Good luck buying a ship from the exchange that isn't very old or total s**t. Also forget upgraded weapons or gear.

In summation, the lack of thought the devs put into this over time, the overbearing intrusive control freaks at CBS/Secret Hideout, and a genuine disregard for the players makes this one a miss for most. If you REALLY love Star Trek and want to play a game with some social elements (oh dear god stay away from Earth Space Dock, it's full of trolls) then you might consider playing this game. 

If you are totally new, just have some honest and realistic expectations that story content and characters will change frequently, voice rolls replaced, and you will need to grind on this like a porn actress for all the premium content you want.

The game doesn't really stay true to Star Trek, the aesthetic is very off and it feels more like a fan fiction that depends on reusing stuff from the old shows constantly to keep fans entertained. The dip in player count shows the lack of enthusiasm its community has had in the game the last few years. 

It is certainly way too centered around constantly fighting, even to a point where you have to do it daily just to grind up fast enough, something common with MMORPGs but strays from the spirit of Star Trek, a series about exploration. 

There is more combat than exploration, more paying to win than earning your way to the top. While there is some exploration, it is either scripted or not thrilling at all, you can just imagine what is going to happen next without having to put much thought in it. Everything up to a certain chapter has been just old characters, enemies and plot lines from the old shows being reused. Don't get me wrong though, the stories are fantastic but they could use a bit more originality, though the fan made ship designs are really cool.

But in summary, the devs really need to put more effort into this game, they did a great job with the recent episodes (except a certain one) but if they want to keep a grip on its withering fanbase, they should take a step in a different direction.

As a lifelong Trek fan, it pains me to see something from this franchise so full of potential yet so devoid of realization.

While I do agree with other reviewers that this isn't exactly the "perfect" Star Trek game (with a balance of exploration, combat, diplomacy, discovery, etc.), I can appreciate what the devs tried to do with this particular vision; and it could have been something... otherworldly... had it not ended up pretty much stagnating.

STO could be an amazing, beautiful game. For the first few years, I enjoyed the presentation, stories and the flow of combat. Of particular note and commendation is the fact that bringing as many original actors from the Trek universe into the game as they could has given it a particular charm that could not otherwise be achieved - it really does make an infinite difference in how the stories are received, and I would not have enjoyed each initial foray anywhere near as much without those iconic presences.

I had enjoyed it so much, initially, that I decided to buy the lifetime subscription. Despite it being easily the most expensive game content I've ever purchased, I did so with the intention of supporting the devs in this project to hopefully make it better. That is not what the money from the lifetime subscription goes to.

The big problem with this title in my opinion is not the mechanics, the (mostly unaddressed / unrepaired) bugs, or the lack of "perfect" Trek balance. The problem is the lack of new content. The only result of spending real cash on a lifetime sub is the devs putting all their effort into new ships to spend MORE real cash on, and little to no actual content. When one looks at any other MMO and the amount of content produced yearly, this one falls incredibly short. I'd be okay with a lack of original actor voices if it meant some decent, sizeable content produced regularly; it wouldn't be as good, but... at least it'd be something. All players get now is event after event of the same few TFO missions endlessly recycled. Why would _anyone_ want to pay huge amounts of cash for ships just to do the same 3 or 4 events over and over again? The devs need to give us reason to WANT to buy new ships and do stuff, and running TFO  for the 16,000,000th time is not gonna cut it AFAIC.

There is also the issue of the "legendary" ships kinda breaking the game for those who have not spent even more money to get them, as they are (from a balance perspective) broken and severely overpowered. This is a much lesser issue, however, and could be remedied by separating legendary and non-legendary players in all content.

For those who might question my review with the sizeable amount of hours sunk into this title... I loved it at first, but now only keep playing every so often to try for the "free" ships offered by event campaigns to feel like I'm getting something - anything - out of my investment into this game.

Best advice I can offer, given STO's current state: play it free, do all the stories and enjoy the actual content that exists, and then consider walking away. As fun as STO can be - and as much untapped potential as it has - "endgame" STO feels like an empty, windowless room, a couple thousand choices of chairs to hoist one's backside upon, and the same 4 songs on endless repeat. Nobody's spending a Saturday evening in a pub like that, y'know?

Star Trek Online is something you can enjoy, but you should also consider its value.

As a fan of the Star Trek universe, you're guaranteed to find something you like here.

The possibilities are there, but not accessible to everyone.

There are tons of starships from all over the galaxy, a large number of story missions with excellent voice acting, and a wide variety of customization options for your captain, bridge officers, and ship.

On top of that, there are PvE and PvP events, seasonal events, fleets with bases, different factions, and much more.

So basically, it's a complete package for all Trekkies.

However, we also have to consider the Gorn in the room: 
FOMO, gacha, pay2win, bugs, and slow hotfixes (if they happen at all).

I'm not someone you can just milk, but I've met many players who, without hesitation, shell out a hundred euros for a ship bundle just to get a single, specific console.

And that's insane, because it's profiting off the backs of people who are ultimately being blackmailed.

It's about maximizing digital "performance," hidden behind a massive paywall.

If it were just about cosmetics, it wouldn't be so problematic in my eyes, but these are items that significantly impact the gameplay experience.

And if enough people have purchased the package, a small patch will often be released to mitigate the "accidentally" overpowered item... 
What a surprise!

The rabbit hole you can climb here is deep if you're looking for optimizing your experience.

Very, very deep.

I mean - watch some videos about top tier builds.

And now, after 15 years of STO, I have to say that the still clunky interface, the truly awful character animations, the disproportionately expensive items in the shop, the terrible communication from the developers (last Steam post from April 25, 2017), the bugs that have persisted for years, the pay-to-win mechanics, and much more,
show how little respect they really have for the fan and player community.

As a fan of star trek it's easy to look at this game and get the occasional shot of nostalgia. From universe accurate weapons, factions, lore, persons of interest, voice acting, sounds, and  music, the game is a nostalgia trip for anyone who has or is exploring the Star Trek Universe.

The good:
 Mechanically, there are two different combat systems:  Sace, and Ground.  Space combat, under most circumstance, is why people play this game.  Space combat, despite mostly being automatic with some offensive/defensive/HOT cooldowns needing to be pressed to to inject some player agency into the combat, is good, and really drives home the game concept, and drama of the setting. There are a number of ships, including famous ships from the series 5 and a half decades long lore, and several small factions you can join, though eventually those smaller factions need to choose to join one of the two larger factions.  Attacks happen in space on a 360 degree ring around your ship, and some weapons have firing arcs, which in turn require you to aim, pivot, and allow you to smartly dodge, or even counter enemies should you maneuver away quickly enough, use appropriate skills, or fly strategically.  Space combat is intuitive under most circumstances, and in a number of situations, the space missions can be varied and interesting, like flying a shuttle through a significantly larger ship to scan and find it's weakness.  That said, most of the missions are generic affairs of "go to system, scan thing 1, fight off 1-2 ships, scan thing 2, fight off 3 ships, scan thing 3 fight off big bad ship while big bad proselytizes at you, and eventually angrily shakes their fist at you while their ship explodes in a generic explody gif, or, if they're romulan, gets resized, and eventually consumed by a rapidly expanding singularity, which eventually explodes in a ring of green generic explody gif.

The Character customization, despite much of it being locked away behind a paywall, and a decade old, is good.  There are several races available each with their own traits (you can even make your own race), and multiple ways which you can customize your Character's outfit, ship, even your Away team/bridge crews outfits, faces, hair styles, even in some cases, their race (if you have an "Alien" bridge officer).



The Meh:
The ground combat, under almost all circumstances, is very bland.  You can choose between a tab targeting style of meh ground combat, or by pressing B, go into a meh and clunky version of third person mouse driven shooter-like combat with powers.  You could be easily deceived that hiding behind cover will protect you.  It will not, and you will primarily be engaging in ground combat via the same combat system utilized in Conan Unchained:  A normal attack that hits one guy, a secondary attack that either hits one guy really hard/stuns/knocks them down or aoe flavor of secondary, While a third attack that in the case of STO, is a melee attack, if you're using ranged weapons.  In the case of melee weapons, it's just Conan Unchained, Left attack, right attack forward swing, in varied flavors based on the weapon in hand.  Much like in space, you have access to powers, heals, grenades, summon more allies, resuscitate fallen away team members, dodge roll, kneel, sprint and aim.  To add to this, your away team NPC allies, have a degree of agency and will randomly throw out their own abilities (grenades, heals, turrets, etc.). 

STO ground combat tries very hard to be something it is not capable of due to old coding, and is mostly okay, just easily forgettable- which is a shame since you will be spending what feels like half of your time kneeling in corridors, and zapping baddies with phasers/disruptors.


The Bad:
From a sub-client launcher, to the antediluvian graphics engine, wonky at best animations, and awkward interface, the game quickly, despite layers and layers of caked on makeup, shows its age.  Character heads are often made of singular polygons, and do not have facial animations.  Character models in cutscenes will emote like NPCs from Fable 1 at you, flailing head, or limbs relentlessly until you finally decide to end their suffering and skip the cutscene, OR will stand there awkwardly seeming to lean forward  as their massive low fidelity forehead takes up 70% of the screen so close that you can count the individual pixels that make up their forehead wrinkles.  Game glitches, like severe rubber-banding, memory leaks, graphical glitches, geometry errors, pathing errors for NPCs/enemies and companions,  seams in maps that players and NPCs alike can fall through, old in game videos, that display these errors, sound/music being poorly balanced, and egregious bad hud design.  I understand that the HUD needs to fit the star trek aesthetic, but it can do so, without being so ugly.

The REALLY BAD:
As you'd assume, there are Three major points of contention with this game:  The Cash Shop, The Publisher, and The Developer.

We'll start with the big one:
The Publisher, is Arc Games.  A publisher that is so universally hated, vilified and  that they had to change their name from Perfect World Entertainment, to Arc Games. Perfect World Entertainment (PWE) has notoriously published, and slowly destroyed such games as Champions Online, Neverwinter, Torchlight, and now Magic The Gathering, through predatory cash shop practices that proceed to whale-bait their clients into spending money.  Several features of the cash shop in STO include, $10-30 purchases of clothing and bridge/duty crew,  $30 purchases of ships, $200 purchases of ship bundles, or fast track content clear tokens costing nearly $100.

Cryptic Studios:
You may know of this company.  A company that has released games that could genuinely be good mmorpgs, Champions Online, Magic The Gathering, Star Trek Online, and Neverwinter.  Both  Star Trek Online, and Neverwinter once had a feature called"The Foundry," that allowed players to create their own in game content such as missions that could span several planets, space combat, political intrigue, and ground combat missions.  This feature was Sunset in 2019 for several reasons.  The most obvious reason was that a player could create a mission that would allow other players to level up rapidly while avoiding the monotony of the in game grind.  So, some players were making missions that could be played on repeat, where you could gun down several ships in a row and level up to cap within a few hours, if that is what you wanted to do, BUT, you still needed to play through the main campaign to unlock new areas and gear.  Alongside Cryptic Studios other games, STO feels like it's always in a state of life support mode, where new content will either be promised and never show up, or come out in such a way that you need to use the cash shop to advance through it in any meaningful way.

The Conclusion (I have no doubt that many people who read this will skip straight here):

I understand that some people, will really love Star Trek Online.  STO is an interesting game with fun lore about Exploring space, seeking out new life and new civilizations and blasting them into an inevitable nuclear winter until they submit to your rule as their federation overlords... or klingon overlords... I'm not judging.  The game has some real fun moments, and some exciting story points (especially the romulan campaign), but beware the publisher.  Arc Games aka "Perfect World Entertainment" is such a predatory company that it makes EA look like an angel.

Would not recommend. While the gameplay and story can be fun enough at first, it quickly becomes extremely grindy and very unfriendly to F2P players. Also, don't expect to set any dps records unless you're either filthy rich, have basically nothing going on to completely no-life the game, or both.
