Throughout its history Star Trek has portrayed an idealistic future where the acquisition of wealth is no longer the driving force of humanity. Star Trek Online shuns this idealistic rhetoric with every fibre of its existence. 

When STO launched in 2010 it had its problems; the Klingon faction was entirely PvP oriented, the graphics were poor, and the missions were bland and boring. Levelling a Federation Character from level one to max was a slog of grinding missions, meaningless combat, and poorly written missions. Levelling a KDF character to max level was even worse. Still, the game had some fun exploration missions for the Federation, even if some became rather repetitive after a while. STO suffered from poor sales with its WoW style monthly subscription, coupled with its grinding issues and poorly balanced factions it soon found itself struggling, despite the strong brand behind it.

STO went Free-to-Play in September 2011. With this came a plethora of gambling mini games using "Master Keys" to open various lock boxes in the hopes of winning an elusive, and oftentimes powerful, Starship. Though some of STO's graphical and gameplay issues resolved over the years, some of the better elements disappeared completely. Exploration and First Contact missions gave way to bad-guy-of-the-week combat missions and poorly rendered cut scenes. It expanded its voice cast to many fan favourites, but that does little to pave over the cracks created by just how Ferengi the game itself feels.

I would not recommend this game. I bought a Lifetime Subscription before launch, so feel more obligated to play it than an actual want to play. It's a mindless grind through a game with the depth of a puddle which barely wastes a chance to prompt its players to gamble on the latest lockbox for a ship people would be more than willing to pay for out-of-pocket.

I can't recommend this game for a new player.

That said, if you're looking to get into Star Trek Online then you should be aware of some major things:

While not exceedingly difficult to pick up at the base level, the game doesn't explain its core concepts very well. Core gameplay is divided between a space component and a ground component. Most people prefer the space component, which is fine, but you will need to do both quite commonly if you're going through the story, and very few aspects of either are explained to the player up front. As such, If you want to do well at endgame, you either need to seek out this information externally, have it explained to you by knowledgeable people, or spend a bunch of time on trail and error in a system that hides or doesn't explain the relationship between different gear and abilities and what best synergises.

There is no 'RPG Trinity' despite what the character class system might appear as. All content is DPS focused, with an admittedly wide variety of methods of achieving that DPS. Tactical Captains (Tacs) Usually boost their damage directly. Engineering Captains (Engs) Indirectly boost their DPS and survivability. Science Captains (Scis) usually debuff enemies to boost their own DPS.'Tanks' and 'Healers' don't commonly exist in game, since while tools exist to facilitate those roles, all content still needs things to die moreso then having people tank or heal.

Outside of the core gameplay, you have a loosely 'Star Trek' themed MMO that will probably appeal to you if you liked the shooty combat parts of Star Trek moreso then the philosophical navel-gazing parts. You can fly virtually any ship in Star Trek canon you can think of, but depending on what ship that is, you might need to spend either significant time grinding out the resources for, or a decent amount of money buying outright, the ship you want.

Ships at endgame are priced at $30 USD for a single ship at baseline price. Sales happen, bundles exist, etc. that let you mitigate costs but for the most part any given ship at endgame is gonna be at least that expensive when no sales are currently running.

You don't really need endgame ships to succeed in most content, thankfully, but if you want the most powerful builds, you will need to buy several ships for the gear and abilities they can give you.

While you can grind out the currency used to buy ships in game, this is a time consuming process that needs significant startup resources to get to be at anywhere resembling a decent income rate. Starting this process from nothing can take you literal weeks of playtime to get to a decent point of income on the resource.

On the brighter side, however, the game typically runs 3 events (Anniversary, Summer, Winter) a year that give out an endgame level ship for doing some daily task or another for a few weeks. These tasks usually take a few minutes, and don't need to be ran on consecutive days.

Character customization is fairly decent, but most outfits will cost you money to acquire, even if many are account-wide unlocks you only need to buy once for your account. The age of the game also shows in many aspects here, however, as despite all the options you can't really do too much with faces.

PvP is virtually non-existent. The devs haven't made it a focus in years, and whatever sort of shenaniganry they put out for PvE use is never checked for what it does in the PvP scene, so if you're looking to have unrestricted PvP that isn't an over-the-top pay to win mess, look for a different game.

All that said, the game is Free To Play if you wan't to try it yourself, but if you want to truly excel at the endgame, you'll likely need to pay out either a decent chunk of money or a significant amount of time.

It breaks my heart to say this, but I can't recommend the game, even from a Free to play angle. 
There was a time where this was THE game I played, it was more then just "My mmo of choice," but the game I spent most of my time playing. Over time though the game has shifted more and more away from a content rich MMO to a more and more grossly priced packages and more predatory gotcha mechanics. 
A clear example is when they took items that used to be free rewards for completing a mission, like unique skins or items, and packed them up into small bundles for real money on the cash shop. 
Sadly it's only gone down hill from there.
Futher more, it's not just the monitization that has gotten worse, but the in game story and features as well. At one time I would have said that STO was worth playing though if you were a Star Trek fan and wanted to experience something other fans had created. While those stories are still in place, including an amazing tribute to DS9, most of the story since that arc have felt like "new trek" that has been shoehorned into the game, complete with newTrek's hallmarks of poor writing, plot-holes, unexplained sudden changes in character and nonsensical outcomes. In once instance, for an entire season a character behaved as a literal war criminal and by the end of their next arc was being held up as a hero for no reason reflected in the script, it literally just happened "because." This is one of many plot points that appear to exist just to inject newTrek content into the game, In one case a long running game figurehead was replaced by a one off Discovery character, who was literally, I shit you not, a zombie woman brought back from the dead using literal magic. This trend is likely to continue as the director behind STO these days has flat said they will continue to chase the shows that are currently on the air rather then let STO make it's own stories.

If this wasn't bad enough, the staff at STO have seemed to stoke a sort of para-social relationship with fans. Case in point, there was a situation not long ago where a week long event was announced that was lauded by the head of social media as "the biggest event in STO history." After a weeks long ARG it was revealed that the "biggest event" was that a handful of ships from STO would be in the background of an episode of Picard. Some people were disappointed and upset, they had been hoping for news relating to the game, an update or a change, a new expansion or perhaps, finally the ability to change our character's gender. I know that I was excited at the idea of an expansion, since every other major MMO was getting a big fun new expansion. Most of us were disappointed.

People who expressed any disappointment were shouted down and the community leader encouraged it by saying that people were being selfish and trying to do a mental 2-step to try and justify the hype.
Since then there as been some quality brought back to the campaign arcs but now they are far more shallow then previously, mostly just a few scant story missions released in clusters about 6 months apart. Before a new story arc would have been a new Reputation line with new gear, a new PvE battle area for all players, 2 new que missions and a line of new ships in the cash-shop rather then in loot boxes exclusively. 

This is the disappointment of  a fan who played at the beta for the game years ago, saw the game make an incredible comeback, release some amazing content and then fall from grace. I hope it can make a comeback again, but the game is getting older every year and some parts are continuing to fall further into disrepair.

STO is unfortunately not a very good game.   It's a collectors hobby with some esoteric niche content for people who have spend the time, effort, and money to build a collection that allows them now to continue to find ways to play.  

Pretty much all the ships you want to fly and use are locked up in gambling boxes that require you to purchase "Keys" to unlock.  You pay to have a near minuscule chance to get what you want.  It's a frustrating nightmare.   Other ships are available for purchase directly, but you're still having to pay money... and rarely are they the kind of ships you nostalgically lust for being a Star Trek Fan... which honestly is the only reason why you're half interested in playing the game in the first place.

Gameplay starts out decent.   with a slow game pace and limited skills that slowly start to ramp up with level unlock.  Equipment is simple and generally intuitive at this point, but once you achieve high level what once was a rather fun game of timing, maneuver, and position is now a skill spam dystopian nightmare of overly complicated traits, equipment, and ability interactions that requires you to build chaining macros to properly activate in sequence to fire off... and the game honestly devolves into having spent enough money for the right 'special' consoles and skill traits, and smashing your macro spam button of choice fast enough.  

Not only this, but game play at the end is so radically different from the start, that leveling to max is nothing more than the prolonged starter instance before you're playing the  'real' game. 

For the good sides, there is an element of puzzling out good combos, trying different set ups and builds on different ships, and the joy of seeing them work... Very little of it feels like Star Trek.   

The ship design is superb, and the design creative and wonderful.  Good enough that many people just collect ships and fly them around purely for the artistic value.   Most of my critic is what you're meant to do with them... and sadly a number of very well known ships are essentially useless for actually playing the game.

There are a number of really engaging story arc missions and narratives that do rise to the occasion.  That are engaging and feel like immersing yourself in a season of Trek... albeit more in a Discovery sort of way with entirely too many epic wars, galaxy ending events only you can stop, and far fewer of the more interesting but more mundane sort of missions that appeal to my personal sensibilities and sense of grandeur.  

End Game Content severely lacks any real prize or reward structure to incentivize or encourage elite content.    Everything you really want is behind a pay to get your chance to play Gambling Monolith known as the Lockbox.  And its all the things behind those paywalls and gambling monoliths that let you play in the only real Endgame... which are the player created DPS leagues.

The greatest single piece of STO was the Foundry, which allowed players to create their own playable missions for other players.  It created a near endless stream of content from truly talented and creative people who were passionate about Trek... and could allow you to build your own piece of the universe as well.    IT was removed when Cryptic became unwilling to continue to keep it up to date, and with it ended the best of the game.

STO was a buggy and unfinished game when it was released... and it's never really recovered from this.  You will find a few individual pieces on the whole that can give you enjoyment, but on the whole it's just flat out not worth it... if you aren't already invested in it.

Anyone who knows me knows I've never been particularly inclined to recommend this game for a number of factors. The game is nice if you like collecting and flying the ships of the Star Trek universe, whether that is the original Constitution to the latest Sovereign class, or fly an iconic ship of the Federation's adversaries from the D7 to the D'deridex, the Galor or the Jem'hadar "fighter." Perhaps you'd rather play a more "common" ship, a workhorse of the fleet, such as the Miranda, Excelsior or the Akira, or maybe an obscure vessel such as the Constellation or the Prometheus. If that is enough to grab your attention, that's plenty.

Star Trek Online has also improved upon its gameplay. Sector Blocks, which have made travel tedious has been replaced with Quadrants. Transwarp to missions have become free, allowing players, especially new players, to reach their objective quickly and easily. Loadout cooldowns have been reduced to allow quick preset changes to your ship instead of waiting a minute or making manual changes. Textures for many starships have been touched up to appear closer to models from shows. Voiceovers from characters like Worf, Seven of Nine, or Odo have been added to the game, allowing players to meet some of their favorite characters.

Having said that, combat has never been a strong point for Star Trek Online. Space combat is fine, but it pales in comparison to other space combat games, even by Star Trek Bridge Commander. Space combat can become complicated by dozens and dozens of abilities to the point where many players, myself included, utilize “keybinds” that allow us to activate many abilities at a moments notice. Ground combat is even worse. Speaking for myself, I found ground combat uncomplicated and dull with only a handful of abilities to use, no cover mechanics, and limited tactical complexity. If you like action, just about any shooter or fighting game will perform better. If you like tactics or strategy, I would suggest also recommend something else.

The Tier 6 ships were of irritation to many players who spent time and money in the purchasing of Tier 5 ships of their choice. When the Tier 6 ships were first released, a lot of players cynically commented about the arrival of Tier 7 ships. While the latter has not technically happened, we now have the release of Legendary Tier 6 ships charging exorbitant rates and bundled in large and expensive packages. Then, there are Ship and Captain Upgrades that push Tier 6 ships to T6-X and provide extra kit and device slots to captains while on the ground. I remember being criticized by another STO player for playing another MMO that was considered “Pay to Win,” yet I see little different. While you can technically buy everything without paying a dime, the game incenses you to pay for loot boxes or expensive packages or risk not getting anything worthwhile. If you want to have “the best ship,” you will absolutely have to pay for it. Fortunately for me, I don’t play this game to be competitive. 

The writing is mediocre, in my subjective opinion, being somewhat simplistic and juvenile. There are a lot more twirling of mustaches in this game than in actual Star Trek, and even those mustache twirlers are intertwined in more complicated situations. Even female changling, who herself is a mustache twirler, seems to have become evil for the sake of being evil, ignoring the complex history of her species, and violate sacred morality set in stone during the narrative of Deep Space Nine.

Having said all that, Star Trek Online is free. Use the reviews to figure out how the gameplay is and ignore polarizing opinions, whether positive or negative, when you can just download the game and try it out at no cost. Beyond that, I would personally recommend against putting money into the game, but that is my personal opinion.

Pros:

lots of space barbie (serious, the options to customize your capt, bridge officers, and ship is paralyzingly deep).

TRIBBLES! tribbles everywhere, and you will need to do pest control of your inventory and banks slots. It's a feature.

Cons:
38+ different currencies not counting craft resources (and better believe you will need know them all).

The grind is real, all those currencies have different task needed to obtain them from the mundane and easy to those you need a guide just to learn even what it's used for, let alone how to get it.

PVP is so unbalanced it's easy to forget that it is even there.

Micro-transactions and lootboxes - lots of them, most of the good things in the game (powerful ship, nice looking outfit, etc.) someone had to buy and is reselling on the in-game market if you didn't buy it with cash (some of the ships go for equivalent of 200 usd).


Lastly, I will admit this is more a personal issue and spite on my part being the main reason I am steering people away. Guilds can be and are hijacked and support will not get involved even when the only reason you can't handle it yourself is because of the system they put in. Beware if you or your friend leave the game for a while, you may return to find some lowlife has gotten top rank and declared themselves ruler of your guild. All they have to do to make it so you can't get rid of them is have 2 or more characters (note: character not accounts they can be on the same account) at max rank, and when you try to force them out they just sign in on the other character and cancel it within 2 weeks. Your only hope of getting your guild back is hope they stop playing, you will need 2 weeks per character at max rank (for example if the have 7 at max rank that's 14 weeks uninterrupted to get your guild back). This has happened to a friend of mine, who lost countless hours in guild resources because he decided to take a break for a few months. 

With how long I've spend playing and fiscally supporting this game I want to give this game a positive review but I can't. Now my wallet is shut and I recommend you think long and hard before investing in this title.

If you choose to proceed: remember check for tribbles before and after any gathering/loot pickup operations, because unaccompanied tribbles are an environmental hazard.
